title: Lamar Jackson holds leverage in contract talks with Ravens. So he's betting on himself Jeff Zrebiec 21

full_text:
Lamar Jackson is set to make $84.3 million next year if the Ravens don't sign him to an extension. Greg Fiume / Getty Images
OWINGS MILLS, Md. — Baltimore Ravens general manager Eric DeCosta had already taken four questions related to his star quarterback’s contract when a slight pause prompted his eyes to dart to each side of the assembled media.
“Any other questions?” he asked last week.
There were. Twenty-two more, to be exact, including a few additional ones on Lamar Jackson. It was fitting that DeCosta’s annual post-cutdown day news conference started with questions about Jackson and ended with one, too.
DeCosta was asked six total questions about Jackson. His responses totaled 154 words, and 47 of those — more than 30 percent — were spent reminding everyone he would not publicly discuss the negotiations.
To put that into perspective, DeCosta was asked one question about last week’s trade of C.J. Okoye, a backup nose tackle who was likely not going to make the team, to the New York Giants — and his answer ran 787 words.
“I’ve said it probably 50 times,” DeCosta said in response to the third query on Jackson. “We are not going to talk about business publicly.”
Jackson, 29, will probably issue the same reminder Tuesday when he’s scheduled to speak to reporters. He’s long declined to discuss his contract situation with the media.
Unfortunately for both, the questions aren’t going away.
A new football season will officially begin for the Ravens on Sunday in Indianapolis, and there is a lot to feel good about. First-year head coach Jesse Minter has brought an open, detail-oriented approach that has quickly resonated with the locker room. There’s confidence that he and Anthony Weaver will fix the defense.
First-year Ravens play caller Declan Doyle has the offense believing it will be explosive and efficient. Jackson has shown full buy-in to the new coaching staff and has spoken boldly about the offense’s potential. Pro Bowl defensive lineman Nnamdi Madubuike is nearing a return, and free-agent acquisition Trey Hendrickson looks healthy and explosive.
Yet, one story hovers over the organization and threatens to mar the good vibes. Without a contract agreement over the next five-plus months — and no outward indication that the two sides have made progress — the speculation about Jackson’s future in Baltimore will get louder and louder.
“The better he plays, the more people are going to focus on it,” said Joel Corry, a former agent who writes and analyzes contracts and the salary cap for CBS Sports. “If he gets back to doing Lamar things, it’s going to be a major storyline. It’s going to gain traction as we go on.”
DeCosta quickly pointed out last week that the Ravens and Jackson have been through this before. He was referring to the tumultuous negotiations in 2022 and 2023 that included a Jackson trade request and months of a standstill, ultimately ending with a five-year, $260 million contract extension on the eve of the 2023 NFL Draft. DeCosta acknowledged after the fact that it was one of the most trying periods of his career.
In many ways, the negotiations this time around could be even more difficult — and the stakes are even higher. As much as the Ravens like to talk about how their competitive window always remains open, the conversation changes significantly if Jackson isn’t on the roster and they need to add a starting quarterback.
“This should be a dictation, not a negotiation, given how this is set up,” Corry said. “If I were Lamar, I’d say, ‘Here’s what I want. If you are willing to do it, let me know. If you don’t want to, that’s fine, too.’”
Under contract through 2027, Jackson has all the leverage. He has a no-franchise-tag clause in his contract, which eliminates one way the Ravens could keep him. He also has a no-trade clause, which means he controls where he could wind up if Baltimore reaches the point where it feels its best option is to trade him.
Meanwhile, Jackson’s salary-cap number grows to $84.3 million next year. That number would make it close to impossible for DeCosta to build a playoff-caliber roster around its franchise quarterback. With Jackson under his current deal, the Ravens are projected to be a league-high $41 million over the cap next year.
That’s untenable, and something has to give. If Jackson is intent on using his leverage to the fullest, the Ravens have no acceptable recourse except to give the quarterback what he wants or to move on from a two-time league MVP without a backup plan in place. The latter is dubious.
“They don’t have any leverage,” Corry said. “Their leverage would come from him having a bad year, and that’s not what they want. They want Lamar to be Lamar, and then they’ll have zero leverage. You’ll have a cap number that you can’t sustain. You can’t franchise him. You need his consent to trade him. Really, Lamar can say, ‘Here’s what I need,’ and what are the Ravens going to do?'”
To be clear, waiting carries some risk for Jackson, too. What if he has a second straight disappointing, injury-plagued year? What if his and the team’s playoff struggles persist?
When he was last available for essentially the price of two first-round picks and a landmark contract, he had no suitors around the league. He wouldn’t carry the draft pick compensation this time around unless the Ravens go the trade route, but he’d be even more expensive — and he’ll also be nearly four years older.
Meanwhile, Ravens owner Steve Bisciotti made clear early in the offseason at the season-ending news conference that the Ravens are prepared and interested in paying Jackson handsomely , and you can bet that DeCosta echoed that sentiment in his talks with Jackson.
Yet a deal didn’t get done in time for the Ravens to gain more flexibility ahead of free agency in March, and the team was forced to execute a contract restructure instead. Barring a late-hour development over the next couple of days, an extension won’t be reached before the start of the regular season. With Jackson serving as his own agent, it seems highly unlikely either side would want the distraction of negotiating a deal in-season.
Thus, the Ravens are nearing a situation that they don’t want to be in, and there’s perhaps more pressure on Jackson to deliver than ever before.
“We have dealt with that distraction before,” DeCosta said last week. “There is only so much we can do.”
What isn’t clear is why the Ravens and Jackson have been unable to gain traction in talks. If you take the word of the Ravens’ top decision-makers at news conferences, the holdup is not a reluctance to go all-in on their end. It makes no sense for them to wait, either.
As for Jackson, it does make sense to wait. Even if his stated desire to remain in Baltimore is genuine, there’s no reason to believe otherwise.
It’s quite possible this was his plan all along as he works toward another groundbreaking deal on his terms. The star-studded 2024 quarterback class, which includes Caleb Williams, Jayden Daniels, Drake Maye and Bo Nix, is eligible for extensions after the upcoming season, and Jackson could wait to see if that resets the quarterback market.
Waiting another year gives him a chance to see how much he likes playing under Minter and how well the Doyle-led offense suits him. Betting on himself and winning big gives him the best chance to get whatever he wants out of the Ravens, too. And let’s be clear: Jackson has never been shy to bet on himself.
Jackson has earned the right to play this out if that’s what he wants. He and his small inner circle have certainly shown over the years that they have a plan. In the meantime, his future in Baltimore will remain the subject of great curiosity and debate, and his weekly performance will be scrutinized for what it could mean going forward.
In other words, what’s been billed as a new era in Ravens football will begin with a familiar question and concern.

title: From DJ Moore to Cole Bishop, 8 Bills who could swing the 2026 season A new No. 1 receiver, a veteran left tackle and young defenders carry big questions — and big stakes — for Buffalo's Super Bowl hopes. Joe Buscaglia 8

The following list isn’t for Josh Allen, James Cook or the known Buffalo Bills players expected to have great seasons or, at the very least, lead the way. This list is about the players slated to have a huge role and at least some volatility in how the Bills’ upcoming season could go.
So, which players
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills are counting on wide receiver DJ Moore and a more explosive downfield passing attack to help fuel their Super Bowl hopes in 2026. Frank Jansky / Icon Sportswire via Getty Images
The following list isn’t for Josh Allen, James Cook or the known Buffalo Bills players expected to have great seasons or, at the very least, lead the way. This list is about the players slated to have a huge role and at least some volatility in how the Bills’ upcoming season could go.
So, which players can help swing the Bills’ season either toward the Super Bowl or below expectations? Here are eight players who can shape 2026.
Without many changes to a passing offense that has been craving an explosive downfield element for the past two seasons, there isn’t a much better example of who could swing the season than Moore.
He was their crown jewel of the offseason, with the Bills effectively spending the last pick in the second round to get him based on the terms of the pick swap. Moore’s contributions to the offense within training camp were immediate and obvious. Allen routinely pushed the ball downfield to Moore, making a concerted effort all summer to build on-field chemistry with the Bills’ new No. 1 receiver.
The Bills brought in Moore to be their No. 1 receiver. The days of “everybody eats” seem to be in the rearview mirror, and it would not be surprising to see Moore on the field constantly and for Allen to default to looking his way. The Bills haven’t had that type of receiver since Stefon Diggs left the franchise. But just because Moore will be on the field a lot doesn’t mean he’ll have the massive impact the Bills are hoping for. After all, Moore’s last two seasons yielded an average of only 824 yards per season. Our film study pointed to perhaps a lack of connection between him and Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams, but you can’t assume Moore will bounce back without question with Allen, even if it looks like a good bet.
A successful season would yield a high snap and target role, while helping to increase the overall depth of target for the rest of the receivers and stressing the defense to create more space.
For as much as Bishop broke out down the stretch of the 2025 season, he isn’t getting talked about as much in the run-up to this season because of all of the newness surrounding the Bills.
His first full year of starting in 2025 began slowly, with inconsistent play but also flashes of great performances in two of the first six games. After the Bills’ bye week, Bishop took off.
From Week 8 through the end of the season in our film study, Bishop very quietly graded out as the Bills’ best defender. He was mostly good to great over all of those outings. His instincts and confidence were outstanding, and his tackling improved, too. Along with his man coverage skills, if he can take that second-half showing and be used creatively within defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard’s new scheme to get around the ball more, Bishop has all the potential to be more than just a good player.
He could become one of the Bills’ best players and make a strong case for an extension. If the end of the season comes and the defense is way better than anticipated, there’s a good chance Bishop had a lot to do with it.
Not a single move — or, in this case, non-move — raised my eyebrows more than the Bills choosing not to convert Dawkins’ 2026 base salary into a prorated bonus.
Why is this important? For context, the Bills were cap-strapped in the offseason, just as they have been almost every offseason since Allen’s massive extension kicked in. Had they converted Dawkins’ salary this offseason, it would have saved them $10.6 million to help their 2026 roster. However, it also would have locked them into keeping Dawkins on the team in 2027 by adding that additional $10.6 million to the cap space they’d need to pay out in the future. By keeping Dawkins’ contract as is, they can get out of the deal next offseason and create $11.2 million in cap space for what is sure to be another cap-strapped offseason.
Though Dawkins had an above-average season in 2025, it was far removed from the dominant player he was in 2024 and still a step down from his 2023 performance. He went through a similar downturn in production in 2022, though not as stark a drop-off as it was from 2024 to 2025.
There was also a key difference: his age. Back around his first dip, Dawkins was only 28, but as a 32-year-old left tackle, it’s a completely different discussion. That’s not to say Dawkins is out of his prime, but he had a large drop in his age-31 season, and the Bills are smartly proceeding with caution.
This is why Dawkins is now one of the sneakiest swing players on the roster. He’s known as one of the best players on the team. He was rated No. 57 in the NFL Top 100 , but I wouldn’t put too much stock in that. I’ve studied every snap of his professional career, and the trio of right guard O’Cyrus Torrence, right tackle Spencer Brown and left guard David Edwards outperformed him in 2024, and none of them were in the Top 100.
Dawkins has been one of the best and most consistent left tackles the Bills have had. This year, Dawkins will have the added challenge of playing next to a first-time starter, Alec Anderson, at left guard. What the Bills will find out is whether Dawkins’ 2025 was a sign of things to come or whether he can find that uptick in production again and help raise the offense’s ceiling.
If there’s one player who can help the Bills’ pass rush to a level that has rarely been seen since Allen arrived, the 22-year-old Walker could be the catalyst. Walker flashes rare ability for a player his size and within Leonhard’s scheme. The Bills have long been searching for a defender who forces teams to game plan for him, and outside of Von Miller for half a season before he suffered a torn ACL, they haven’t had that player consistently.
Walker has been a presence in the backfield and has notably gotten better at the point of attack during practices, but that’s just practice.
The biggest hurdle for Walker will be minimizing those fleeting moments in run support that were a slight issue as a rookie. Still, he has all the makings of someone who can make defenses account for him, and perhaps help unlock the explosive Ed Oliver working alongside him.
Many things are different about this year’s defensive scheme, and one is that the Bills are far more likely to play man-to-man coverage under Leonhard. What would help is if one of their two young cornerbacks hits and becomes their locked-in starter opposite No. 1 boundary cornerback Christian Benford. The Bills are giving Hairston, their top draft pick in 2025, every chance to be that guy to begin the season. They haven’t ruled out a platoon strategy between Hairston and rookie second-round pick Igbinosun, though it remains to be seen if they’ll go through with that in Week 1. All we know is that Hairston will be the “starter.”
The trouble here, though, is that Hairston had a fairly uneven summer. He struggled in coverage and physicality throughout and suffered a groin injury that forced him to miss practice time, and that follows a rookie year with inconsistent tape but some big flash plays that show his potential. The No. 2 cornerback role is such an unknown that how those two young players perform can shape how offenses attack the Bills through the air. The Bills are keeping their fingers crossed that Hairston or Igbinosun becomes that answer.
From an injury perspective, it’s been a frustrating first few years to begin Kincaid’s career, and his on-field role has suffered as a result. Despite that, Kincaid concluded perhaps the healthiest camp he’s had since his rookie year; he performed very well and had a big role in the Allen-led offense during open practices.
If Kincaid can become a 60 to 65 percent snap player, be just competent enough in blocking to preserve the threat of play action when he’s on the field and continue to crush receiving…

full_text:
Bears coach Ben Johnson won't let his team dwell on its 2025 success. "No," he says, "we're resetting it back to square one, and we have to build our way back up." Kamil Krzaczynski / Imagn Images
LAKE FOREST, Ill. — Someone asked Chicago Bears general manager Ryan Poles if he ever worried about how Ben Johnson would handle success.
The first-year head coach led the Bears to their first playoff win in 15 years, after all. There might have been a little mystery, at least to those who don’t know him well.
“No,” Poles told The Athletic in his office last month, “because it’s always about this massive goal, ambitious goal — it’s always going to be out there.”
One trait that separates his coach is the ability to realize each year is its own chapter, that it’s going to be a different team. And Johnson has made sure everyone in the building gets on board.
“I appreciate his leadership on that because that mentality allows you to, I think, keep stacking year after year after year,” Poles said. “Because no one’s satisfied.”
The son of a coach who has been a coach in the NFL since 2012, Johnson didn’t necessarily have a mentor who showed him how to react to a season-ending loss. He didn’t have a specific experience that led him to set the tone from the start: that 2026 would be different and that resting on the laurels of a division title wouldn’t do anyone any good.
“I recognize that last year was a cool season. OK? It was for the players, for the staff, for the city,” Johnson told The Athletic . “I recognize that, and I don’t want to downplay that. That was an incredible experience, something that I will never forget.
“At the same time, I also know recent history in Chicago has been, you can have a flash-in-the-pan season, and then the next season it (disappears). You know? We don’t want that. Nobody wants that.”
That’s been Poles’ goal since he arrived in 2022 — sustain success. Sure, it’s every GM’s ambition, but Poles also studied up on his new team when he arrived. He saw a franchise that hadn’t had back-to-back playoff seasons in what’s now been 20 years.
Now he has a head coach who certainly has the play-calling acumen to end that drought as well as the leadership qualities.
“He does not have the mentality of it just rolls to the next year and things just happen the way they did a year prior,” Poles said. “So that desire to be great, reinvent ourselves, create the identity each and every year, that to me is the part where I really believe we’re in a good spot.”
Poles said he felt Johnson’s message “went through the locker room immediately.” He noticed a commitment from the building. More players worked out at Halas Hall during the downtime than Poles had seen before. He’d see social media posts of teammates traveling with quarterback Caleb Williams to get in extra throwing sessions.
“There really was no space for satisfaction of winning a playoff game or almost winning a divisional game or being close to a championship,” he said, “and that was my biggest fear because it’s been so long that you would have some people take a deep breath like, ‘Oh, you know, we’re OK now.’
“(Johnson) nipped that immediately and you felt it go through the whole organization, which was awesome.”
The season opener is Sunday on the road against the Carolina Panthers, the official start of the 2026 season and the moment the page has truly been turned. Johnson has generally not been interested in entertaining questions about last season. What happened against the Los Angeles Rams in the divisional round of the playoffs won’t affect what happens against the Panthers on Sunday.
That tone was set after a cold night full of emotions in January.
One day after the Bears lost to the Rams, Johnson offered the message of reality to his team.
“We go back to square one,” he told them. “It’s back to the bottom again, and we got to build this thing back up.”
Johnson said he’ll “never forget” the two home playoff games. “Just the energy, the vibe — you could feel that,” he said last January after the overtime defeat.
But he wouldn’t linger on it, and he wouldn’t let his players, either.
Minutes after Williams’ final pass was picked off, creating the opportunity for the Rams’ game-winning field goal, tight end Cole Kmet had already refocused his mind.
“It starts all over,” he said after the game. “It’s 0-0, and it’s gonna be twice as hard to get to this point, you know? … To just think that it’s just gonna happen again, that’s very wishful thinking, very wishful.”
Seven months later, Kmet reflected on the experience he felt as a rookie, joining the Bears in 2020 and hearing players still talk about 2018. Two years is a long time in the NFL, yet that wild-card loss to the Philadelphia Eagles still stung in the building.
A lot of “what could have been” from the team’s previous division title still permeated.
When the Bears traveled to Cincinnati for a joint practice last month, Kmet noticed how much the Bengals’ defense changed in one offseason, a perfect example of the message Johnson is sending.
“You’ve got to understand how this league’s structured as they want seven to eight, nine new teams to be new playoff teams each and every year,” Kmet said. “It’s the reality of it. So when (Johnson) says that stuff, like to me, that rings true.”
The Bears, for example, have 20 players on their Week 1 53-man roster who weren’t part of things at Halas Hall last season. They can’t speak to how exhilarating the season was, or how disappointing the end was.
Some coaches might use a spring and summer to put together a kicking competition to make sure a playoff miss won’t happen again. But Johnson didn’t spend all offseason rewatching Williams’ interception and wondering how close they were to the NFC Championship Game. That wouldn’t have been productive.
As much as the interception still “burns,” Williams told a small group of reporters, and “still bothers me today,” he followed his coach. He moved on.
“Obviously when you’re reading a book, you don’t forget the last page,” Williams said. “So you remember the page and it helps for the pages to come after and what’s going to happen at the end of the book. Like Ben said and like Ben has been saying, we’re on to the next and we’re going to try to focus on being able to this year get past that game and go further than we did last year.”
Johnson is never satisfied. He has lofty goals. He is hypercompetitive, but not in the mindset of obsessing over a loss from the previous season — instead, it’s making sure that no one is assuming a return to that playoff environment is a given.
The idea of a “lull” can’t happen under his watch.
Wide receiver Kalif Raymond was with the Detroit Lions with Johnson and head coach Dan Campbell. They won back-to-back division titles together.
“You win a division, people are gonna play harder against good teams,” Raymond said. “It always happens. … I mean it’s just a part of the game; it is part of human nature. And it’s part of being a great coach to be like, ‘Hey, man, there’s a lull if you get trapped in that.’ But more importantly, you can always use this from a mental perspective.”
Quarterbacks coach J.T. Barrett was also with those winning Lions teams, and he won plenty as a quarterback at Ohio State.
“We’re still hunting, but at the end of the day having that mentality like, ‘Hey, what you’ve done doesn’t matter anymore. You still have to go out there and rebuild your reputation, your identity as a team, and what you want to do,’” Barrett said. “And so I think that’s our game, and that’s just how it works.”
Guard Jonah Jackson, another former Lion, looked at Johnson’s turn-the-page lesson as pragmatic. You can’t change the past, he said. But it can still fuel you.
“Things like that in games where you’re right there have only made us better and made us more hungry for what’s to come,” he said.
It’s striking how seldom the interception has popped up in any conversations. The miraculous touchdown to Kmet no longer became a…

title: Bengals' Zac Taylor knows there's pressure, and he wouldn't want it any other way Expectations are high and the criticism is getting louder as Taylor tries to get Cincinnati back to the playoffs after a three-year absence. Paul Dehner Jr. 10

CINCINNATI — The tunnels inside Paycor Stadium are a cacophony of chaos, as the sounds of construction crews, stadium workers and golf carts mix with music blasting from the home locker room.

full_text:
Zac Taylor starts his eighth season as Cincinnati Bengals head coach on Sunday at home against the Buccaneers. Kirk Irwin / Getty Images
CINCINNATI — The tunnels inside Paycor Stadium are a cacophony of chaos, as the sounds of construction crews, stadium workers and golf carts mix with music blasting from the home locker room.
Zac Taylor decides to dip into a quiet, soundproof room to talk. That’s the default setting of the Cincinnati Bengals head coach, after all. Always has been — this time of year, more than ever.
Block out the noise. Isolate to the task at hand.
The task at hand in this specific moment is a sit-down with this reporter, followed by an overdue meeting with offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher to clean out the back of the call sheet.
Broadly, though, the task at hand is to take arguably the best roster assembled in the Joe Burrow era and create a connected team capable of capturing the first Lombardi Trophy in the franchise’s 59 years of existence.
For nine months, piece by piece, the stars have aligned for Taylor. He’s surrounded by more than $200 million in defensive investments, five returning starters on the offensive line, a traditionally stable division in unprecedented transition, one of the easiest schedules in the NFL, preseason health, complete staff continuity, Year 2 of his defensive coordinator change and an OC in line for head coach jobs.
Oh yeah, and a 6-foot-5, 350-pound franchise-changer in Dexter Lawrence at the center of it all.
Every move along the way increased the font size on the key Bengals headline for 2026: Can Taylor make this happen? What happens if he can’t?
His seat, as they say, is hot.
“Sure,” Taylor said instantly at the first mention of the concept. “Always.”
Indeed, the headline is not new. Taylor went to a Super Bowl and back-to-back AFC Championship Games in 2021 and 2022, coming off a 6-25-1 start to his coaching career. But any credit for him was eclipsed by the blinding rise of Burrow and Ja’Marr Chase. Even those successes are now outshone by three straight seasons outside the playoffs, including 6-11 last year, his first losing campaign since the postseason runs.
Even for an expert isolationist in his eighth season, blocking out every snippet of doubt, criticism and first-coach-fired odds becomes impossible as the pressure mounts around a season of immense expectations.
“The ones that get you — this happened last night — ‘Hey, don’t listen to what people are saying. You’re doing a great job,’” Taylor said with a laugh. “OK. I don’t know what people were saying. Thanks for bringing it up, though.”
For a 43-year-old head coach who came up as the quarterback at Nebraska, where “you could hear people booing you mid-play,” he wouldn’t want it any other way. That’s precisely why he’s surrounded by a building of believers betting his leadership can take the Bengals back to SoFi Stadium.
“You have to coach every single day like your career is on the line,” Taylor said last year. “Pressure is not the word I like; it’s just the job. And that’s what I like about the job. I don’t want anybody else to have this job. I want it.”
In 2026, he’s coaching to keep it.
What’s being said about him rarely seeps through traditional avenues. No, it’s often the ones closest who spring a leak.
Like when Taylor was driving with his son, Brooks, this spring and the voice of Stephen A. Smith popped on the radio.
“‘Do you like Stephen A. Smith?'” Taylor recalled Brooks asking.
“I was like, you know what I respect? He has to talk about a lot of topics and be knowledgeable on it, then you’re not gonna have a home run every time,” Taylor said. “So I respect the work he does.”
Brooks wasted no time reaching his point: “Well, he said you should be fired.”
“I was like, ‘well, I don’t agree with that one,’” Taylor said.
The Bengals front office didn’t, either, despite extreme fan frustration surrounding Taylor and de facto general manager Duke Tobin in the aftermath of last year’s disappointment.
Bengals president Mike Brown issued a statement backing both Taylor and Tobin days after the season. It served as half-support, half-warning. Taylor has two years left on his contract, but it’s fair to say that it might not matter if another season of prime Burrow is wasted.
Everyone in the front office commenced doing their part. The organizationally unprecedented Lawrence trade — giving up the No. 10 draft pick in return — was the main event in an aggressive investment to fix the defense and keep the offense intact. They even paid $6 million to Joe Flacco as Burrow injury insurance.
“The front office has taken a lot of heat from the fans, the public, the media,” Burrow said in June. “We can put all of that behind us. They went and made it happen.”
Tobin’s approval rating spiked after one of the most locally popular offseasons in recent history. That turned the other half of the equation over to Burrow and Taylor. Burrow called it the most talented roster he’s had around him since joining the Bengals and made comparisons to his 2019 Heisman and national championship season at LSU, something he’d never done before.
Taylor didn’t mind the amplification of expectations. He wants players who put in the work to feel confident enough to speak freely, chief among them his franchise quarterback.
However, everyone knows that if this season fails, nobody will blame Burrow. Success or scapegoat will fall to the head coach.
As for those first-coach-fired odds, Taylor ranks third at 7/1 behind the New York Jets’ Aaron Glenn and the Washington Commanders’ Dan Quinn. Despite his best efforts, he’s heard about those, too.
“I know what it looks like when it’s good and that’s what you’re fighting for,” he said. “You just want to replicate that and go beyond it. And so it’s worth being in a situation where people are gonna judge you and say terrible things to you and about you. It’s worth it because if you do the good things, it’s tenfold the opposite direction.”
Taylor might work to stay insulated from national opinion, but he feels the local ones. He knows expectations have never been higher around here because people tell him as much. They do so at any and every youth sports field, restaurant, fundraiser or school function.
His two boys, Brooks and Luke, and two younger girls, Emma Claire and Milly, have grown up here. He and his wife, Sarah, are part of the fabric of the community.
Delivering for this place means more than it did when the transient football coach and his young family arrived in 2019.
“I don’t know if it’s just ’cause I live here, but Cincinnati is such a small city,” Taylor said. “I feel like it really will affect every human here in a really positive way.”
Taylor takes a 13-minute drive down Columbia Parkway to Paycor Stadium in the early hours every morning. He does so in silence.
He says the time is reserved to remind himself what the organization needs from him that day.
The result creates what his staff views as the defining character trait of his coaching style and antidote to dealing with every extreme-pressure situation.
“Anytime anybody has ever asked me about Zac, to me, the first attribute that I always mention is consistency,” said Pitcher, retained from Marvin Lewis’ staff and with Taylor since his first day. “That is a critical attribute, I think, for any leader. For anybody who works under him and for the whole staff, I just think there is such ease when the leader is consistent and you know what the environment is going to be and that is the same when times are good and times are bad. You know what to expect, that is a very conducive environment to produce your best work.”
Staff movement in Cincinnati is glacial — and also an organizational standard. The only major move on his coaching staff in eight years was parting ways with longtime defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo following 2024.
Despite going 6-11 and finishing in third place last season, all but one coach on staff returned under Taylor. Nearly half of his…

full_text:
Jared Verse was part of Cleveland's trade haul for Myles Garrett. Nick Cammett / Getty Images
The Cleveland Browns are initiating yet another reset after a tough 5-12 finish in 2025. They fired Kevin Stefanski and traded two-time Defensive Player of the Year Myles Garrett, who had been with the franchise since he entered the league in 2017.
In comes Todd Monken, a longtime offensive coordinator, as the new head coach in Cleveland. Monken has decided to stick with Deshaun Watson as his QB1, a move that has confused and enraged some of the fanbase . Watson, who missed the entire 2025 campaign due to an Achilles injury, has yet to appear in more than seven games in a single season since 2020. Considering the Browns’ history at quarterback , chances are that Shedeur Sanders will get another shot at some point this fall.
There are promising talents around the rest of the roster. Monken gets to work on passing concepts with first-round draft pick KC Concepcion and second-rounder Denzel Boston. Alongside those rookie receivers is Harold Fannin Jr., the breakout tight end entering his second season. The left tackle spot is now shored up by No. 9 pick Spencer Fano, a unanimous first-team All-American from Utah.
Garrett will be missed on defense, but the Browns landed standout edge rusher Jared Verse in that trade with the Los Angeles Rams. Verse joins proven players like cornerback Denzel Ward and safety Grant Delpit. Reigning Defensive Rookie of the Year Carson Schwesinger can build upon his impressive debut at linebacker as well.
Still, there are a lot of questions surrounding this team. Unfortunately for fans, finding out how to watch every game is one of them. That’s why we’ve compiled a TV guide that works whether you’re from Cleveland or are supporting the Brownies from afar.
Make sure you’re following the Browns on The Athletic . No matter what the quarterback situation looks like, beat reporter Zac Jackson will provide the latest on the Dawg Pound.
All times listed below are ET.
The most expansive option for live game coverage is a multichannel plan. That includes streamers like Fubo, Sling TV and YouTube TV, or more traditional providers like DirecTV, Dish and Xfinity. We lay out cord-cutting alternatives for each NFL media partner down below, but there’s a certain peace of mind to the consolidation of pay television.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, AFC Championship Game
Each week, CBS carries games across two Sunday kickoff slots: one at 1 p.m., and another at 4:05 p.m. or the national window at 4:25 p.m. There will be 10 nationwide Sunday doubleheaders this year on CBS. Broadcasts are set by region when there are multiple offerings in a spot.
It’s not a clean split, but CBS is known as the primary home of the AFC. The network’s theme music is a certified slapper.
Its main pregame show, “The NFL Today,” adds recent retirees Russell Wilson and Kyle Long to its studio crew. CBS announcers include Jim Nantz and Ian Eagle, while the color commentary rotation stars JJ Watt.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an indoor TV antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local CBS games also stream on Paramount+.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, NFC Championship Game
Like CBS, Fox splits Sunday afternoons between early 1 p.m. action and later 4:05/4:25 p.m. matchups. Its centerpiece is branded as “America’s Game of the Week.” Unlike CBS, Fox has a dancing robot named Cleatus . It’s the nominal network for the NFC as well.
Kevin Burkhardt, Joe Davis and Adam Amin are the lead play-by-play voices. Burkhardt pairs with Tom Brady, while Davis calls games alongside Greg Olsen. Amin is partnered with newcomer Drew Brees, who is fresh off his Pro Football Hall of Fame induction. Some Spanish-language broadcasts are available on Fox Deportes.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local Fox games also stream on Fox One.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (out-of-market fans)
These two are the access points for all non-national matchups that aren’t on regional CBS or Fox.
NFL Sunday Ticket has full games. It’s exclusive to YouTube and YouTube TV. Those without a YouTube TV plan can still get NFL Sunday Ticket as a primetime channel through the standard YouTube app.
RedZone is the whip-around program that jumps around the slate to cover scoring drives. This is the place for Scott Hanson , “the witching hour” and chaotic octobox split screens. It can be added to NFL Sunday Ticket, and it’s included on some high-end pay TV sports plans.
RedZone also lives on NFL+ Premium, which can be bundled with the ESPN Unlimited plan.
What you’ll need to watch: An NFL Sunday Ticket subscription through YouTube TV or the YouTube app; NFL RedZone access through select pay TV packages, ESPN Unlimited or NFL+ Premium.
Playoffs: 2 wild-card games, 1 divisional game
This is the faithful home of “Sunday Night Football” each weekend. And because everything has to be confusing, the NBC lineup opens with a Wednesday night season premiere. At least SNF has a consistent 8:20 p.m. start time.
Mike Tirico and Cris Collinsworth are in the booth, with Melissa Stark reporting from the sidelines. Carrie Underwood sings about waiting all day for Sunday night . NBC’s “Football Night in America” pregame show brings on longtime head coach Mike Tomlin. Telemundo has the telecasts in Spanish.
The network has two extra Saturday offerings for Week 17. One is exclusive to Peacock, and both matchups will be announced later in the season. The same goes for NBC’s Week 18 regular-season finale.
“Sunday Night Football” is subject to flex scheduling — games can be swapped in and out of the window twice between Weeks 5-10 and any time from Weeks 11-17. This allows executives to pick games with greater playoff implications, though it leaves the actual ticket holders in a bind.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing, or a Peacock account with the live sports plan.
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, Super Bowl LXI
The Disney networks combine to cover 17 “Monday Night Football” games. Ten of those are on both ABC and ESPN, with another seven exclusive to the latter. The oft-maligned “Monday Night Football” doubleheader is now a thing of the past.
MNF kickoffs have 8:15 p.m. starts, and their schedule flexes can happen any time in Weeks 12-17. The two Saturday ABC/ESPN matchups in Week 18 will be set as the postseason picture sharpens.
ESPN is preparing for its first Super Bowl broadcast ever on Feb. 14, 2027. It will be simulcast on ABC.
Joe Buck handles play-by-play for MNF. He’s joined by analyst Troy Aikman, plus the sideline duo of Lisa Salters and Laura Rutledge. Spanish-language airings can be found on ESPN Deportes. For 12 regular-season games and the Super Bowl, ESPN2 offers an alternate “ManningCast,” in which Eli and Peyton Manning watch the games with famous fans. Guests have ranged from Bill Belichick to Lil Wayne .
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for ABC, or an ESPN Unlimited account.
Main window: Thursday night
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game
Most weeks begin with “Thursday Night Football,” which kicks off at 8:15 p.m. Those games are behind the Prime paywall, but they’re free over the air in the participants’ home markets. Flex rules around TNF are a bit less hectic, with two allotments between Weeks 13-17.
The Browns are set to appear on TNF once this season when they host the rival Pittsburgh Steelers in Week 4.
Thursdays are called by Al Michaels and Kirk Herbstreit, with Kaylee Hartung on sideline duty. Herbstreit loves dogs ; Michaels hates vegetables . Prime has Spanish-language coverage and advanced stat broadcast options within its app. Among the pregame and postgame personalities are former All-Pros Tony Gonzalez, Richard Sherman and Andrew…

summary:

There’s always new energy with a new head coach. There was a seismic roster shift in June, five weeks after another intriguing draft class arrived. There was also a double down by team ownership on the current front office in early 2026.
Later this week, we’ll start to see what kind of product a Cleveland Browns franchise in transition puts on
full_text:
Browns rookie receivers KC Concepcion, left, and Denzel Boston are two playmakers who should be heavily involved on offense. Diamond Images / Getty Images
There’s always new energy with a new head coach. There was a seismic roster shift in June, five weeks after another intriguing draft class arrived. There was also a double down by team ownership on the current front office in early 2026.
Later this week, we’ll start to see what kind of product a Cleveland Browns franchise in transition puts on the field in a season that begins with low external expectations but warranted optimism for the future.
Ready for some season predictions, areas of concern, a fair look down the road and an honest glimpse at what’s right in front of the Browns? Here we go with a list of 26 such things, an homage to the year 2026 and 26 being the number of losses the Browns have suffered over the past two seasons.
26. I’m fairly certain the Browns open the 2026 season wishing there was a fast-forward button to 2027. What looks to be another strong draft class has arrived, but this is a future-focused project that likely won’t compete for the postseason. Team owner Jimmy Haslam acknowledged as much at the start of training camp, though he said he’d “ take the over ” on the projected season win total of 5.5.
25. Can this team really win six games? I tend to think it can’t, but there’s a fair amount of mystery involved. If the folks in charge really fixed the offensive line, maybe new coach Todd Monken’s offense can create big plays and support a defense that still has top talent. The Browns have added playmakers and strengthened an impressive young core. But Myles Garrett is gone — defensive mastermind Jim Schwartz is, too — and they have to play six of their first nine games on the road.
24. This is a rebuilding project. No one dazzled in a quarterback competition that Monken let play out deep into August despite always leaning toward Deshaun Watson’s experience. Watson hasn’t played in two seasons, hasn’t been good in six seasons and is only signed through this year. So why would one of the league’s youngest teams go back to a player who’s previously failed the franchise? Only Monken and those atop the organization know the answer. They also seem to be the only ones who think going back to Watson is a good idea.
23. The current outlook is somewhere between bleak and cloudy, but this is not 2016. The Browns have some young talent, headlined by the top of the 2025 draft class: Mason Graham, Carson Schwesinger, Quinshon Judkins and Harold Fannin Jr. The Browns insisted upon getting Jared Verse back as part of the Garrett deal. As many as five 2026 rookies could be full-time players soon, and rookie receivers KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston were summer stars .
22. General manager Andrew Berry and his staff have done a good job cleaning up their own mess caused by the 2022 Watson trade sinking the ship. The offensive line remake is on — really, the whole offense is in transition — and the Browns, partially by design and partially by necessity, will be one of the league’s youngest teams.
21. With a young roster and first-timers at head coach and in all three coordinator spots, this could be a fascinating experiment. It could be revealing on multiple levels. Could it be another outright disaster? Given the state of the quarterback position and the lack of proven depth, the Browns could end up being really bad again.
20. Maybe that’s OK. Maybe that’s actually the goal. I don’t think we’re going to see outright tanking, and obviously no one involved has talked about that being the plan. But let’s see where things stand after the Browns host the Pittsburgh Steelers in a short-week situation in Week 4, then travel to play the New York Jets in Week 5. By then, we’ll know a whole lot more about the 2026 Browns than we currently do.
19. What are realistic goals in Cleveland right now? Develop young talent. Identify areas of strength and weakness. Perhaps continue to acquire another young piece or two, but development and evaluation must be paramount before the Browns make big draft and contract-related decisions over the next 20 months.
18. In an ideal world — and in the bigger picture — the growth of this core would make up for the growing pains that surely will be a part of this season. Maybe there’s a part of the blueprint that says the folks in charge head to 2027 feeling pretty good about almost every position group except quarterback. Maybe that’s actually close to attainable.
17. After he was booed in a home preseason game last month, Watson said he wasn’t sure if he could handle the negativity and said he might have to approach the season like there are 17 road games. Two days later, he was announced as the starter. The inability to stay physically healthy has been a big part of Watson’s trouble during his Cleveland tenure, but can we really be sure he’s mentally ready to make a successful comeback?
16. The football gods usually watch non-Browns games on Sunday (and who could blame them?), but they have a sense of humor. We’re headed for Watson versus Baker Mayfield in Week 2, and we can only hope the CBS cameras get good looks at pregame on-field interactions and the visiting team’s owner’s box during the game.
15. The way for all involved to avoid (or at least temper) an all-time awkward situation for Watson and the franchise in Cleveland’s Week 3 home opener would be for the Browns to win one of their first two games in Florida. Just play well and find a way to win. Folks will start to believe if they see Monken and the young playmakers putting out a watchable and competitive product.
14. The Browns have led the NFL in punts in two straight seasons, and last year Corey Bojorquez had 15 more punts than the player with the second most. The Browns were 31st in the NFL in scoring last season and last in 2024. I think “watchable” is a fine place to start in the season directly ahead.
13. Defensive stalwarts Denzel Ward and Grant Delpit got extensions in July, and Ward looked like the best player on the practice field throughout training camp. The Browns now have the 2024 NFL Defensive Rookie of the Year in Verse, and last year’s top defensive rookie, Schwesinger. Graham looks like a quicker, more confident player in his second season.
12. After the Buffalo Bills came to town for an August joint practice and quarterback Josh Allen looked like the All-Pro passer he is in every competitive drill, Allen told reporters he still believed the Browns would have a strong defense and pointed out that Schwesinger wasn’t participating in the practice. “He’s a stud,” Allen said. “He’s gonna be really good for a long time.”
11. Verse isn’t Garrett. No one is. But Verse is one of the strongest players the Browns have ever employed, and he’s heading toward a mega-extension after the season because the folks in charge believe Verse will be disruptive on the field and be the kind of leader they need in the locker room.
10. It’s hard to know exactly what to expect from the Cleveland defense under new coordinator Mike Rutenberg. The attack-style scheme is the same, but there will be structural tweaks. Opponents used to start thinking — well, worrying — about Garrett on Mondays, and that continued all the way through Sunday’s game. The pass-rush group isn’t nearly as scary without Garrett, and that could affect every level of the defense.
9. If the defense is strong and Judkins drives the ground game, the Browns could find some early wins. From sideline (and occasional bleacher) observation, the most noticeable difference from Augusts of the recent past was the playmaking ability of the young receivers. Concepcion and Boston both appear NFL-ready and will be heavily involved.
8. Last year, the pass game was bad in every aspect outside of Fannin being much better than anyone expected. Concepcion and Boston might cut into Fannin’s overall opportunities, but Fannin is still really good — and needs to be…

title: Broncos get first shot at rehabbed Patrick Mahomes. Can they bring heat on Chiefs' QB? The Broncos have sacked Mahomes 10 times across the past three meetings — but they are still searching for a first road win vs. KC's QB. Nick Kosmider 1

full_text:
The Broncos aren't viewing Patrick Mahomes' return from injury any differently from other times they've faced him. "It’s still Patrick Mahomes, at the end of the day,” Patrick Surtain II said. Jamie Schwaberow / Getty Images
ENGLEWOOD, Colo. — Patrick Mahomes watched the game from a suite high above the field at Arrowhead Stadium the last time the Denver Broncos were in town. The Kansas City Chiefs quarterback was 10 days removed from major surgery to repair ligaments in his left knee. He could only fidget on Christmas night as Kansas City, guided by third-string quarterback Chris Oladokun, lost on its home field to the Broncos for the first time in a decade.
Less than 10 months later, the two-time league MVP will no longer be a spectator. The Broncos will be the first team to face rehabbed Mahomes when they visit the Chiefs for the final game of the Week 1 schedule Monday night. They don’t envision the three-time Super Bowl champion, who didn’t play in the preseason, easing his way off the starting line during his highly anticipated return.
“Coming off an injury like that is pretty tough, but I don’t expect anything less from him than to be himself,” All-Pro cornerback Pat Surtain II said. He added, “It’s still Patrick Mahomes, at the end of the day.”
Mahomes has largely been a Broncos antagonist since making his first NFL start in Denver to close the 2017 season. He has never lost to them at home as a starter — a perfect 7-0. The Broncos, though, have won four out of the last five games overall between the two teams, including two of three when Mahomes started. The Broncos in those three games have sacked him a combined 10 times and limited him to 42 total rushing yards. Mahomes has thrown two touchdowns and three interceptions while posting a 77.2 passer rating in his last three starts in the series. Denver has pressured him on 38.7 percent of his dropbacks in that stretch. It’s a major reason Mahomes has stared at an average distance to gain on third downs of 7.4 yards.
In short, coordinator Vance Joseph’s defense has routinely disrupted Mahomes in recent matchups. The sample is too small, though, for the Broncos to believe they have figured out a quarterback who led Kansas City to the AFC West title in his first seven seasons as a starter before last year’s 6-11 flop.
“I think we’re looking at it and expecting someone who’s 100 percent, someone who’s moving well based on what limited footage you get,” Broncos coach Sean Payton said. “He’s going to be one of those guys that threatens you not only in the pocket but out of the pocket. So our approach has been to pay close attention to what we’ve seen historically film-wise, how we defend not only him, but their team.”
One issue for Mahomes during his recent dip in performance against the Broncos is he hasn’t been supported by a strong running game, making it easy for Joseph to send an array of pressure looks the quarterback’s way on all downs. No running back for the Chiefs in Mahomes’ last three starts against the Broncos has rushed for more than 59 yards. It was part of a broader trend that saw Kansas City rank 31st among NFL teams across the past two seasons in yards per carry by running backs (3.7).
Enter Kenneth Walker, the reigning Super Bowl MVP, who joined the Chiefs in free agency after four years with the Seattle Seahawks. The last time the Broncos faced Walker came when they visited Seattle for the 2024 season opener. He rushed 20 times for 103 yards, and 81 of those yards came during a third-quarter flurry that flipped the game for the Seahawks.
“He’s an elite back in this league,” Broncos linebacker Alex Singleton said. “He really takes the ball anywhere on the field on any given play. You can’t just, like on a stretch play, set the front side. You’ve really got to have containment on the backside — and really all over. It really forces all 11 guys on the defense to be able to tackle him.”
The Broncos, their struggles against Walker two years ago aside, rank first since the start of the 2024 season in TruMedia’s defensive rush success metric, limiting opposing running backs to 3.9 yards per carry. The matchup against Walker is an early test for a defense that enters the season without edge-setter Jonathan Cooper, the outside linebacker currently on the commissioner’s exempt list as he awaits trial on an assault charge. Controlling that battle will be key in Denver’s quest to test Mahomes’ mobility with various pressure looks — as they did while sacking him three times during his start against the Broncos in Denver in November.
Mahomes, of course, is not the only quarterback returning from injury in this matchup. Broncos starter Bo Nix will be playing in his first real game since suffering a broken ankle in a January playoff win against the Buffalo Bills. The third-year quarterback has deftly handled the pressure from Chiefs defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo. He has posted a 108.8 passer rating in four matchups, Nix’s highest mark against any of the six teams he has played more than once in his career. Still, for all the quarterback has seen in his career, the atmosphere at Arrowhead on Monday will be a significant test for Nix in his first regular-season game working with Davis Webb as the offensive play caller. The Chiefs, as Mahomes put it earlier this offseason, will be aiming to rid themselves of the “bad taste” of a lost season. Payton expects nothing less than a menacing environment to greet his quarterback.
“Steve has always done a great job disguising looks, giving you zone-pressure looks,” Payton said. “He’s not afraid to play zero (coverage). You’re going to have to have a real good protection plan and be disciplined in your approach, especially when you’re facing that defense on the road with the noise.”
Mahomes and Nix appear set to battle each other at or near the top of the AFC West for the foreseeable future. The result of the next installment in this budding rivalry could come down to which player can most efficiently handle his return after an offseason of rehab.
Veteran safety Taylor Rapp signed with the Broncos’ practice squad Monday. He was on the field as the team began its preparations for the Chiefs, less than two weeks after Denver released him so he could attend to a personal matter.
Rapp, who has played seven NFL seasons with the Los Angeles Rams and Bills, initially signed with the Broncos on Aug. 20 after a tryout with the team. When the Broncos released him six days later, Payton said Rapp needed “a little time at home” and added there was a “better than good chance” the veteran would ultimately be back with the Broncos — and he was after another tryout over the weekend. To make room on the practice squad, the Broncos cut backup long snapper Luke Basso.
The Broncos already have a plan for their Week 1 practice squad promotions, fullback Adam Prentice and long snapper Mitchell Fraboni, so Denver would need to create a spot on the active roster for Rapp if it wanted him to suit up for the opener.

full_text:
Jahmyr Gibbs has shared the backfield with David Montgomery in the past but will take on a larger workload with Montgomery gone. Junfu Han / Imagn Images
ALLEN PARK, Mich. — The Detroit Lions have assembled one of the most talented rosters in football. But as we saw last year, talent can only get you so far.
Health, quality depth, growth from young players — all necessary. Across the board, really.
But when evaluating this team, certain positions give you pause. The Lions need favorable outcomes there more than others. They’re the groups that, in many ways, could make or break the season.
If you’re not used to seeing the running back position here, grab a ticket and join the line. For three consecutive years, the Lions had the best RB tandem in the NFL. Jahmyr Gibbs and David Montgomery combined for 7,652 scrimmage yards and 82 touchdowns in the regular season during their run in Detroit. You could sleep peacefully knowing the Lions were in good hands at one of the most injury-prone positions in football. But that sense of security is now one play away from vanishing.
Montgomery is off to the Houston Texans after an offseason trade. The team hoped to account for Montgomery’s departure by signing Isiah Pacheco to a one-year deal, but Pacheco missed weeks of practice with a sprained MCL, then picked up a back injury. He’ll miss at least the first four games of the season after being placed on injured reserve. There is no timetable for his return.
This is life in the NFL, but the Lions were living a sheltered one for years. They’ll lean on Gibbs as their bell-cow running back, and after last season, it’s wise to do so. He’s the most explosive back in football, and he’s signed for the long haul . But at 5-foot-9 and 202 pounds, is Gibbs built to handle a top-five workload? He ranked 17th in attempts per game in both 2024 and 2025. He’s young enough to handle more, but it does give you a bit of pause. If Gibbs goes down, the Lions will be left with Sione Vaki (seven career carries) and Jacob Saylors (two career carries), with Pacheco out. They no longer have the luxury of Montgomery.
Gibbs is tougher than he looks for a smaller back and has proven to be durable throughout his career, but it’s at least worth mentioning as he takes on a new role with more touches. This offense runs through him.
This offseason, the Lions promptly addressed an offensive line in need of retooling. They moved on from veterans Graham Glasgow and Taylor Decker — replacing them with Cade Mays (three-year, $25 million contract in free agency) and first-round pick Blake Miller. Penei Sewell moved from right tackle to left. Second-year guard Tate Ratledge is back for more. And the Lions brought in veteran Ben Bartch to compete with left guard Christian Mahogany, and Larry Borom as starting-caliber depth at tackle.
Where does that leave the room now that the season is almost here?
Mays is shelved until mid-October at the earliest . The Lions are rolling with Juice Scruggs — who reacclimated to center in training camp — until further notice. Miller went through predictable rookie struggles in camp, and the Lions didn’t make it much of a battle, relegating Borom to the second-team offense early in camp. Bartch missed extended time with a foot injury and a concussion. Without the necessary practice time to compete for the left guard job, Mahogany enters the year as the default starter. If Miller looks like a rookie, Scruggs can’t hold up at center and Mahogany and Ratledge don’t take the necessary leaps, this unit could look a lot like it did last year. We saw how that went.
If you’re an optimist, you’ll buy that Miller, whose growth from OTAs to training camp has been praised, will only improve as he gains valuable game reps. His athleticism will be an asset in the screen game and on tackle pulls, which we’ve already seen in practice. Settling the right tackle job early in camp allowed Miller to develop chemistry with the starters and gives you a veteran backup in Borom who knows his role. Mays offers the size and anchoring ability in the interior the Lions covet. He should be able to protect Jared Goff in ways the Lions couldn’t last year. His backup, Scruggs, is a natural center who might’ve started over Glasgow a year ago. Ratledge is looking like an ascending player in his second year, mentioned in the same breath as core players by coach Dan Campbell. Mahogany, despite not being pushed, has looked the part in his third year and will be playing alongside an All-Pro in Sewell and an upgrade at center in Mays when he returns.
Which version of the offensive line will we get? The answer will go a long way toward determining how efficient this offense is.
Three of Detroit’s four 2025 starters in the secondary — four of five if you include the nickel position — won’t take the field for the Lions in their season opener Sunday against the New Orleans Saints. Amik Robertson left for the Washington Commanders in free agency. Former first-round pick Terrion Arnold was arrested and released this offseason. And starting safeties Kerby Joseph (knee) and Brian Branch (Achilles) will begin the year on IR and miss at least the first four games. Naturally, it’s created some uncertainty.
D.J. Reed returns as the lone holdover as a starting outside corner — in the second year of a three-year, $48 million contract. After dealing with a hamstring strain last season, the Lions need Reed to play like a CB1. He had been one of the league’s most consistent cornerbacks prior to arriving in Detroit, so the talent is there. We have to see it in 2026.
Rock Ya-Sin is the projected starter opposite Reed. After signing a one-year deal with the Lions in 2025, Ya-Sin performed above expectations — allowing a passer rating when targeted of 74.1 across 16 games. The question with Ya-Sin will be consistency. He’s 30, and the position is volatile. Can he provide the same baseline of play over 17 starts?
And finally, at safety, the Lions are patiently waiting for Branch and Joseph to return. When might that be? Depends who you ask. Campbell initially thought Branch and Joseph would return to practice in late August or early September. We’re on the tail end of that window now, and Lions general manager Brad Holmes didn’t have an updated timetable for either player. They’re not eligible to play until October, anyway.
Best-case scenario: The supporting cast of Chuck Clark, Avonte Maddox and Roger McCreary hold down the fort until Branch and Joseph return. Reed plays up to his contract. Ya-Sin offers excellent value as a CB2. Branch looks like himself immediately, giving the Lions an All-Pro-caliber DB. Joseph, even if he has to manage his knee, is still capable of creating turnovers and forcing QBs to second-guess throwing his way. The Lions have more than enough in the secondary.
Worst-case scenario: Reed struggles again. Ya-Sin’s production declines when asked to play more snaps. Clark and Maddox are liabilities at safety. Branch struggles to shake off the rust. Joseph’s knee remains an issue. QBs feast on this secondary.
Given the secondary concerns, the Lions could need a big year from their defensive line — making it one of the most important groups on the roster. You could say that every season, of course, but the Lions haven’t had depth like this every season.
Aidan Hutchinson, at this stage of his career, is a perennial 12-sack, 100-pressure performer when healthy. That feels like the baseline. He hit 14.5 sacks last season, and could’ve had more if not for some sack-negating penalties. What he offers in the room makes life easier for those around him. The Lions believe they have the necessary pieces around him.
DJ Wonnum gives them a high-floor, veteran edge who can do a little bit of everything. The last time Wonnum played with an edge like Hutchinson, he turned in a pair of eight-sack seasons with the Minnesota Vikings, along with above-average run defense. Wonnum says this is the best training camp he’s had in…

full_text:
Jonathan Taylor led the league in both rushing touchdowns and first downs last year. Boris Streubel / Getty Images
The Indianapolis Colts went through an anticlimactic end to a promising 2025 campaign. But with a healthy squad again, they could be ready to return to playoff football.
It looked like they would get there last season during an 8-2 start. Then Daniel Jones, who was in the midst of a bounce-back year, went down with a torn Achilles in Week 14. Indianapolis finished on a seven-game losing streak. Now the question is if Jones and the team can get back to their early-2025 ways under head coach Shane Steichen.
Star running back Jonathan Taylor returns on a new two-year extension after he led the NFL in total touchdowns, rushing touchdowns and first downs. He’s the league’s active leading rusher in yards per game with 90.5.
Alec Pierce also signed a contract extension in the offseason, moving into the WR1 role after the Colts traded Michael Pittman Jr. to the Pittsburgh Steelers. Pierce ranked first among all receivers in yards per reception in both 2024 and 2025. He’s once again joined by Josh Downs out wide, with veteran Keenan Allen as a new target for Jones.
On defense, Sauce Gardner and Charvarius Ward combine to form a menacing secondary, while Laiatu Latu continues to show flashes off the edge. He’s heading into his third season after leading the team with 8 1/2 sacks in 2025.
Indianapolis has plenty of can’t-miss games this season, including a Week 2 road matchup against the Kansas City Chiefs and a trip to London in Week 4. Unfortunately for fans, catching the action has become increasingly difficult thanks to new streaming deals and subscription plans. Regardless of where you’re tuning in from, our guide to watching the Colts throughout the regular season has you covered.
Before getting into the broadcast schedule, make sure you’re following the Colts on The Athletic , as well as the stellar work of beat writer James Boyd .
All times listed below are ET.
The most expansive option for live game coverage is a multichannel plan. That includes streamers like Fubo, Sling TV and YouTube TV, or more traditional providers like DirecTV, Dish and Xfinity. We lay out cord-cutting alternatives for each NFL media partner down below, but there’s a certain peace of mind to the consolidation of pay television.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, AFC Championship Game
Each week, CBS carries games across two Sunday kickoff slots: one at 1 p.m., and another at 4:05 p.m. or the national window at 4:25 p.m. There will be 10 nationwide Sunday doubleheaders this year on CBS. Broadcasts are set by region when there are multiple offerings in a spot.
It’s not a clean split, but CBS is known as the primary home of the AFC. The network’s theme music is a certified slapper.
Its main pregame show, “The NFL Today,” adds recent retirees Russell Wilson and Kyle Long to its studio crew. CBS announcers include Jim Nantz and Ian Eagle, while the color commentary rotation stars JJ Watt.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an indoor TV antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local CBS games also stream on Paramount+.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, NFC Championship Game
Like CBS, Fox splits Sunday afternoons between early 1 p.m. action and later 4:05/4:25 p.m. matchups. Its centerpiece is branded as “America’s Game of the Week.” Unlike CBS, Fox has a dancing robot named Cleatus . It’s the nominal network for the NFC as well.
Kevin Burkhardt, Joe Davis and Adam Amin are the lead play-by-play voices. Burkhardt pairs with old Colts rival Tom Brady, while Davis calls games alongside Greg Olsen. Amin is partnered with newcomer Drew Brees, who is fresh off his Pro Football Hall of Fame induction. Some Spanish-language broadcasts are available on Fox Deportes.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local Fox games also stream on Fox One.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (out-of-market fans)
These two are the access points for all non-national matchups that aren’t on regional CBS or Fox.
NFL Sunday Ticket has full games. It’s exclusive to YouTube and YouTube TV. Those without a YouTube TV plan can still get NFL Sunday Ticket as a primetime channel through the standard YouTube app.
RedZone is the whip-around program that jumps around the slate to cover scoring drives. This is the place for Scott Hanson , “the witching hour” and chaotic octobox split screens. It can be added to NFL Sunday Ticket, and it’s included on some high-end pay TV sports plans.
RedZone also lives on NFL+ Premium, which can be bundled with the ESPN Unlimited plan.
What you’ll need to watch: An NFL Sunday Ticket subscription through YouTube TV or the YouTube app; NFL RedZone access through select pay TV packages, ESPN Unlimited or NFL+ Premium.
Playoffs: 2 wild-card games, 1 divisional game
This is the faithful home of “Sunday Night Football” each weekend. And because everything has to be confusing, the NBC lineup opens with a Wednesday night season premiere. At least SNF has a consistent 8:20 p.m. start time.
Mike Tirico and Cris Collinsworth are in the booth, with Melissa Stark reporting from the sidelines. Carrie Underwood sings about waiting all day for Sunday night . NBC’s “Football Night in America” pregame show brings on longtime head coach Mike Tomlin. Telemundo has the telecasts in Spanish.
The network has two extra Saturday offerings for Week 17. One is exclusive to Peacock, and both matchups will be announced later in the season. The same goes for NBC’s Week 18 regular-season finale.
“Sunday Night Football” is subject to flex scheduling — games can be swapped in and out of the window twice between Weeks 5-10 and any time from Weeks 11-17. This allows executives to pick games with greater playoff implications, though it leaves the actual ticket holders in a bind.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing, or a Peacock account with the live sports plan.
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, Super Bowl LXI
The Disney networks combine to cover 17 “Monday Night Football” games. Ten of those are on both ABC and ESPN, with another seven exclusive to the latter. The oft-maligned “Monday Night Football” doubleheader is now a thing of the past.
MNF kickoffs have 8:15 p.m. starts, and their schedule flexes can happen any time in Weeks 12-17. The two Saturday ABC/ESPN matchups in Week 18 will be set as the postseason picture sharpens.
ESPN is preparing for its first Super Bowl broadcast ever on Feb. 14, 2027. It will be simulcast on ABC.
Joe Buck handles play-by-play for MNF. He’s joined by analyst Troy Aikman, plus the sideline duo of Lisa Salters and Laura Rutledge. Spanish-language airings can be found on ESPN Deportes. For 12 regular-season games and the Super Bowl, ESPN2 offers an alternate “ManningCast,” in which Colts legend Peyton Manning joins his brother Eli to watch the games with famous fans. Guests have ranged from Bill Belichick to Lil Wayne .
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for ABC, or an ESPN Unlimited account.
Main window: Thursday night
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game
Most weeks begin with “Thursday Night Football,” which kicks off at 8:15 p.m. Those games are behind the Prime paywall, but they’re free over the air in the participants’ home markets. Flex rules around TNF are a bit less hectic, with two allotments between Weeks 13-17.
The Colts currently have one Thursday night game: on the road against the rival Houston Texans in Week 11.
TNF is called by Al Michaels and Kirk Herbstreit, with Kaylee Hartung on sideline duty. Herbstreit loves dogs ; Michaels hates vegetables . Prime has Spanish-language coverage and advanced stat broadcast options within its app. Among the pregame and postgame personalities are former All-Pros Tony…

full_text:
With Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes returning from December knee surgery, their offensive line depth is a major concern. Nathan Ray Seebeck / Imagn Images
We’re less than a week away from the Kansas City Chiefs’ “Monday Night Football” opener against the Denver Broncos, so let’s go over three things I think about the team before the season kicks off.
It feels like we talked all offseason about the Chiefs’ question marks at wide receiver.
Very quickly, though, K.C. has had a much more dire issue emerge: the depth — all over — on the offensive line.
It started in the preseason. The Chiefs made it clear they weren’t sold on their interior backups when they kept rotating tackles Jaylon Moore and Kahlil Benson to the interior during drills when right guard Trey Smith sat out with a back injury. In late August, it seemed likely K.C. would look to the trade market to address this need, and sure enough, it acquired New York Giants guard Joshua Ezeudu to help.
Since then, though, the offensive line situation has gotten only worse. Left tackle Josh Simmons has remained out and away from practices with a back injury, leaving his immediate availability in doubt.
The Chiefs swung another trade for Baltimore Ravens left tackle Diego Pounds, but he doesn’t profile as a quick solution after just picking up the playbook. Without Simmons, the Chiefs will likely look to Moore at left tackle and Benson at right tackle — the latter of whom would be quite a story, per TruMedia, as only two undrafted rookie tackles have started Week 1 of their first season since 2000.
Just five months ago, general manager Brett Veach acknowledged that any time he mentioned potentially drafting a first-round right tackle before the NFL Draft , it was only as a smokescreen.
Life has come quickly at the Chiefs since then. Offensive tackle has to be considered their biggest worry heading into Week 1, and the overall O-line depth also remains a major concern, especially with quarterback Patrick Mahomes returning from December knee surgery.
From the early portions of training camp , it was obvious the Chiefs were repping more under-center plays than in past seasons.
Now we have some small-sample data. And it all points to K.C. looking to unlock free-agent running back Kenneth Walker III — and more of its play-action game — with a shift toward more non-shotgun plays.
Per TruMedia, the Chiefs went under center on 20 percent of their snaps in 2025. During three preseason games, that rose to 31.1 percent — and even came with Walker getting extremely limited playing time.
The Chiefs view Walker as a three-down back , and his vision and burst have played up best when he has been able to run from under center. That scheme type also allows for greater versatility in runs.
I wouldn’t expect the Chiefs to finish in the top half of the NFL in under-center plays, especially with other teams likely to increase their own usage after the Rams’ recent success with that setup.
It seems clear now, though, that this will be a greater part of the Chiefs’ repertoire as they look to play to their personnel’s strengths.
This won’t be a surprise if you saw my bold prediction for the Chiefs earlier this week.
But third-year receiver Xavier Worthy is getting overlooked — and I’ll go bold enough to say he’ll get to 1,000 yards this season.
Part of this thought goes back to the 2025 NFL combine, which was after Worthy’s rookie season. I asked coach Andy Reid then about Worthy’s potential, and Reid said he was excited to expand on what Worthy had shown in the playoffs.
“He’s not the biggest guy, but he’s not afraid to run crossing routes. Sometimes you see those guys and they tiptoe across. He goes 100 miles an hour, man,” Reid said in February 2025. “All the stuff he did was all new compared to what he did in college. So we’re seeing it, and then for Pat to be able to trust and know where he’s going to be … all that stuff takes time. So, that’s a great thing.”
That was all going to set up a potential breakout 2025 season — before Worthy collided with tight end Travis Kelce and tore his labrum in the season opener. Though Worthy returned to the field, he wasn’t himself, and Reid later acknowledged the Chiefs changed his route tree to reduce injury risk. Specifically, they stopped using Worthy on those crossing routes Reid was so excited about before the season.
All that’s worth considering for Worthy, who is still only 23 and younger than rookie receiver Cyrus Allen.
Worthy was the team’s MVP during summer practices , when he flashed as a home-run threat again with his elite speed. He also says he has benefited this offseason from working with a more detail-oriented receivers coach in Chad O’Shea.
Injury has to be the biggest concern here, and Worthy missed most of training camp after reinjuring his shoulder. He’ll be full-go for Week 1, and though Worthy’s a small guy at 5 feet 11 and 165 pounds, he wasn’t injury-prone in high school or college; that could give some hope that last year’s season-altering ailment was more of a fluke than a trend.
I was surprised to see betting markets put Worthy’s expected receiving season total around 650 yards — lower than Kelce’s.
Health will be something to watch. But if Worthy is out there and can get back to his full route tree, I see him surpassing that 650 number easily.
