Every​ week during the season, Chad Graff and Josh Kendall rank and analyze all 32 teams from first to worst.
At long last, the NFL season has arrived. The excitement kicks off with a Super Bowl rematch Wednesday night between the New England Patriots and Seattle Seahawks. The next day, the Los Angeles Rams will face the San Francisco 49ers in
full_text:
Sean McVay's Rams seem to have the makings of a Super Bowl champion. Can all of his stars shine in Los Angeles this season? Ronald Martinez / Getty Images
Every​ week during the season, Chad Graff and Josh Kendall rank and analyze all 32 teams from first to worst.
At long last, the NFL season has arrived. The excitement kicks off with a Super Bowl rematch Wednesday night between the New England Patriots and Seattle Seahawks. The next day, the Los Angeles Rams will face the San Francisco 49ers in Australia. After that, the normal Sunday slate awaits.
As the season opens, let’s jump into our first power rankings since before training camps began while also considering each team’s projected win total, as provided by our analyst Austin Mock.
Are you ready for some football?
First game: vs. 49ers (in Australia), Thursday, 8:35 p.m. ET
Mock’s projected win total: 11.7
The Rams easily got the most projected wins in Mock’s simulation despite playing in arguably the best division in football. That presumed success is for obvious reasons. They traded for Myles Garrett and Trent McDuffie, then brought back arguably the best defensive tackle of all time in Aaron Donald. They’re officially a superteam.
First game: vs. Patriots, Wednesday, 8:20 p.m. ET
Mock’s projected win total: 10.9
How do you win the Super Bowl, return a very similar roster with the same coach and not be the No. 1 team? Well, that says less about the Seahawks and more about the Rams. Seattle’s defense should be incredible again, but the big question is how Sam Darnold and the offense look after losing offensive coordinator Klint Kubiak, who became the coach of the Raiders.
First game: at Texans, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Mock’s projected win total: 10.8
The defense is undergoing a significant change, entering a 3-4 scheme with six new starters, and that’s part of the reason for hope. The other is a fresh start with coach Joe Brady that could get this team over the hump and into the Super Bowl. Even if last season didn’t go as planned, it’s hard to keep a Josh Allen-led team out of the top five entering the season.
First game: at Seahawks, Wednesday, 8:20 p.m. ET
Mock’s projected win total: 10.3
The Patriots went to the Super Bowl, then meaningfully improved an offense that returns the MVP runner-up at quarterback (who just turned 24, by the way). Still, this team benefited from a historically easy schedule a year ago. So what’s on tap for this new group that added receivers A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs? How about opening with games against the Seahawks, Steelers, Jaguars and Bills (with three of them on the road). No more schedule complaints this season.
First game: at Chiefs, Monday, 8:15 p.m. ET
Mock’s projected win total: 9.1
It’s hard to know what to make of the Broncos. On the one hand, they almost went to the Super Bowl, even while playing a backup quarterback in the AFC Championship Game. Their coach is an offensive genius, and they return an excellent defense. On the other hand, they play in a difficult division, and we’re supposed to just believe that Bo Nix, who relies on his mobility, is going to return to a high level of play after a pair of offseason ankle surgeries?
First game: at Rams (in Australia), Thursday, 8:35 p.m. ET
Mock’s projected win total: 10.1
There was no shortage of offseason storylines around the 49ers, including the arrest of their owner and a car accident that injured coach Kyle Shanahan. They also dealt with a number of offseason injuries. But they’ve gotten good news of late with George Kittle and Christian McCaffrey, and they could use the regular season to get back up to speed after so much drama.
First game: vs. Bills, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Mock’s projected win total: 9.3
There’s no defensive line in the NFL more feared than the Texans’, which boasts an embarrassment of riches after adding Jadeveon Clowney to a group that already featured Will Anderson and Danielle Hunter. So we know the defense should be very good. The big question is what can C.J. Stroud do in Year 4 after his 2025 campaign ended with a terrible playoff performance. They may have to win games 17-14.
First game: vs. Cardinals, Sunday, 4:25 p.m. ET
Mock’s projected win total: 9.4
It wasn’t a great August for the Chargers, who lost center Tyler Biadasz to a season-ending ACL tear. In their second preseason game, they had as many punts (eight) as first downs. But star offensive tackles Joe Alt and Rashawn Slater enter the season healthy, and it’ll be fun to watch this offense under new coordinator Mike McDaniel.
First game: vs. Saints, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Mock’s projected win total: 10.3
After missing the playoffs last season, the Lions will benefit from one of this year’s easiest schedules. The division will be tough, but they have a new offensive coordinator in Drew Petzing and more depth on the defensive line. Still, the secondary could have some struggles early due to injuries to Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph, each of whom begins the season on the PUP list.
First game: at Panthers, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Mock’s projected win total: 9.5
There are questions on defense about the pass rush and depth on the back end after Coby Bryant’s injury. But Caleb Williams is promising, and Ben Johnson seems like the real deal, so how far can the offense carry this team? If Dennis Allen can manufacture some pressure, this could be a really good team.
First game: at Colts, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Mock’s projected win total: 11.0
The Ravens actually have the second-highest projected win total in Mock’s model, but we had a hard time getting them into the top 10 with all of the unknowns. Can Lamar Jackson stay healthy? Can new coach Jesse Minter return the defense to elite status? We’ve bumped them up five spots since camp started given their good health and easy schedule to start the season.
First game: vs. Commanders, Sunday, 4:25 p.m. ET
Mock’s projected win total: 10.4
A pair of joint practices in New England didn’t go well for the Eagles offense, which dealt with wide receiver injuries in training camp and a learning curve under new coordinator Sean Mannion. That, of course, sets up an important season for Jalen Hurts, who threw more interceptions during camp than you’d like. Still, the defense should be good, and the running game has a high floor.
First game: vs. Browns, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Mock’s projected win total: 9.1
It’s easy to forget that this team won 13 games last season, and that was without do-it-all 2025 No. 2 pick Travis Hunter for much of the year. He lined up on defense more than offense in training camp, but we can expect a bounce-back season from the Heisman Trophy winner. Still, questions exist for the running game after the departure of Travis Etienne in free agency.
First game: vs. Broncos, Monday, 8:15 p.m. ET
Mock’s projected win total: 9.6
Our last power rankings assumed Patrick Mahomes would probably miss the start of the season. Astoundingly, even though he suffered an ACL tear in mid-December, it looks like he will be the Chiefs’ starting quarterback out of the gate. There is still plenty that ailed the Chiefs a year ago (and could again this year), but it’d be wise not to bet against Mahomes.
First game: at Giants, Sunday, 8:20 p.m. ET
Mock’s projected win total: 9.2
The Cowboys have a loaded offense and should be fun to watch, but there are still plenty of questions on defense. New defensive coordinator Christian Parker learned under Vic Fangio in Philadelphia, and that unit added Rashan Gary in free agency, then Caleb Downs and Malachi Lawrence in the first round of the draft. If the defense can turn it around, Dallas could surprise some people.
First game: vs. Buccaneers, Sunday, 1 p.m. ET
Mock’s projected win total: 10.3
Thanks in part to arguably the easiest schedule in the league, the Bengals open the season as favorites in 15 of their 17 games. The defense got some meaningful improvements in the offseason (notably by uncharacteristically trading for Dexter Lawrence), but their season will once…

full_text:
De'Von Achane is averaging a fantastic 5.6 yards per carry since entering the league in 2023. Rich Storry / Getty Images
“Miami Dolphins, Miami Dolphins! Miami Dolphins No. 1.”
That earworm aside, the Dolphins might not really be No. 1 this year. But they are committing to a new era, with a blank canvas to work with in the games to come.
First-year head coach Jeff Hafley arrives after his solid stint as the defensive coordinator for the Green Bay Packers. Malik Willis is the starting QB, joining Hafley in relocating from Green Bay to Miami Gardens. The incoming rookie class includes first-round draft pick Kadyn Proctor along the offensive line and Bronko Nagurski Trophy winner Jacob Rodriguez at linebacker.
Miami’s production once again funnels through thrilling running back De’Von Achane , who plays far beyond his 5-foot-9 frame. He led the NFL at 5.7 yards per rush last season. He also stretched out the sidelines as a true three-down receiving option. Achane looks to keep building in his age-25 campaign, running behind second-team All-Pro center Aaron Brewer.
The Dolphins are going to be tested from the jump with three road games through Week 4. Patience is needed here, but long-term viewer payoff is certainly within reach. This fall’s updated schedule and broadcast partners can be found down below. Follow the Phins on The Athletic to keep up with everything, too.
All times listed below are ET.

Its centerpiece is branded as “America’s Game of the Week.” Unlike CBS, Fox has a dancing robot named Cleatus . While it’s the nominal network for the NFC, it’s where you can find the most Dolphins games this year. That includes Miami’s Week 15 road trip to Green Bay to face Hafley’s old team.
Kevin Burkhardt, Joe Davis and Adam Amin are the lead play-by-play voices. Burkhardt pairs with Tom Brady, while Davis calls games alongside Greg Olsen. Amin is partnered with newcomer Drew Brees, who is fresh off his Pro Football Hall of Fame induction. Some Spanish-language broadcasts are available on Fox Deportes.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local Fox games also stream on Fox One.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (out-of-market fans)
These two are the access points for all non-national matchups that aren’t on regional CBS or Fox.
NFL Sunday Ticket has full games. It’s exclusive to YouTube and YouTube TV. Those without a YouTube TV plan can still get NFL Sunday Ticket as a primetime channel through the standard YouTube app.
RedZone is the whip-around program that jumps around the slate to cover scoring drives. This is the place for Scott Hanson , “the witching hour” and chaotic octobox split screens. It can be added to NFL Sunday Ticket, and it’s included on some high-end pay TV sports plans.
RedZone also lives on NFL+ Premium, which can be bundled with the ESPN Unlimited plan.
What you’ll need to watch: An NFL Sunday Ticket subscription through YouTube TV or the YouTube app; NFL RedZone access through select pay TV packages, ESPN Unlimited or NFL+ Premium.
Playoffs: 2 wild-card games, 1 divisional game
This is the faithful home of “Sunday Night Football” each weekend. And because everything has to be confusing, the NBC lineup opens with a Wednesday night season premiere. At least SNF has a consistent 8:20 p.m. start time.
Mike Tirico and Cris Collinsworth are in the booth, with Melissa Stark reporting from the sidelines. Carrie Underwood sings about waiting all day for Sunday night . NBC’s “Football Night in America” pregame show brings on longtime head coach Mike Tomlin. Telemundo has the telecasts in Spanish.
The network has two extra Saturday offerings for Week 17. One is exclusive to Peacock, and both matchups will be announced later in the season. The same goes for NBC’s Week 18 regular-season finale.
“Sunday Night Football” is subject to flex scheduling — games can be swapped in and out of the window twice between Weeks 5-10 and any time from Weeks 11-17. This allows executives to pick games with greater playoff implications, though it leaves the actual ticket holders in a bind.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing, or a Peacock account with the live sports plan.
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, Super Bowl LXI
The Disney networks combine to cover 17 “Monday Night Football” games. Ten of those are on both ABC and ESPN, with another seven exclusive to the latter. The oft-maligned “Monday Night Football” doubleheader is now a thing of the past.
MNF kickoffs have 8:15 p.m. starts, and their schedule flexes can happen any time in Weeks 12-17. The two Saturday ABC/ESPN matchups in Week 18 will be set as the postseason picture sharpens.
ESPN is preparing for its first Super Bowl broadcast ever on Feb. 14, 2027. It will be simulcast on ABC.
Joe Buck handles play-by-play for MNF. He’s joined by analyst Troy Aikman — who was hired by the Dolphins as a consultant earlier this year — and the sideline duo of Lisa Salters and Laura Rutledge. Spanish-language airings can be found on ESPN Deportes. For 12 regular-season games and the Super Bowl, ESPN2 offers an alternate “ManningCast,” in which Eli and Peyton Manning watch the games with famous fans. Guests have ranged from Bill Belichick to Lil Wayne .
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for ABC, or an ESPN Unlimited account.
Main window: Thursday night
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game
Most weeks begin with “Thursday Night Football,” which kicks off at 8:15 p.m. Those games are behind the Prime paywall, but they’re free over the air in the participants’ home markets. Flex rules around TNF are a bit less hectic, with two allotments between Weeks 13-17.
Thursdays are called by Al Michaels and Kirk Herbstreit, with Kaylee Hartung on sideline duty. Herbstreit loves dogs ; Michaels hates vegetables . Prime has Spanish-language coverage and advanced stat broadcast options within its app. Former Dolphins quarterback Ryan Fitzpatrick is one of the pregame, halftime and postgame personalities.
What you’ll need to watch: Amazon Prime. TNF is also free on Twitch with a registered account.
The league-owned media outlet is now under ESPN’s purview, thanks to a blockbuster deal that gave the NFL a 10 percent ownership stake in “The Worldwide Leader in Sports.” As of July 30, NFL Network is integrated into the ESPN Unlimited plan. It can also be accessed through NFL+ or NFL+ Premium.
NFL Network has five of the international games, plus a pair of Saturday matchups in Week 16 to be revealed…

full_text:
Justin Jefferson of the Vikings is one of the NFL's best wide receivers, but what makes him great? His wide receivers coach goes to the film to explain. Elsa / Getty Images
EAGAN, Minn. — The film pauses, and Keenan McCardell uses a green laser pointer to circle a New Orleans Saints defender on the projector in front of him.
“At the time,” McCardell says, “this was a matchup .”
It’s the week before the 2026 season, and McCardell, the Minnesota Vikings’ wide receivers coach, is acing the assignment. I want to know what impresses him most about superstar receiver Justin Jefferson, his longtime pupil. What clips would he, a two-time Pro Bowler for the Jacksonville Jaguars and Tampa Bay Buccaneers, show to introduce Jefferson’s exceptionalism to the average fan?
He has been going for more than 15 minutes. But now he is spotlighting former Saints cornerback Marshon Lattimore from a 2022 game in London.
“He doesn’t ever talk about these matchups,” I say.
“We don’t talk about them,” McCardell says. “Ever.”
“They’re just X’s,” McCardell says. “I never talk about them. In my room, it’s never, ‘All right, you’re facing such and such.’”
Once more, McCardell outlines Lattimore on the screen with his laser pointer.
“Look at his technique,” McCardell says. “Beat his technique. Counter his technique. Don’t give them power. You’ve got the power.”
Did you learn that somewhere?
“That’s just how I played,” McCardell says. “It’s just how we go about it. Growing up, being a receiver, I always felt like I was in control of where I put the defensive back. I always used to say, ‘I can put the DB wherever I need him to be so that I can get open.’ That was my mindset. If you’re a dominant receiver, dominant route runner, that’s the mindset you’ve got to have.”
He’s standing up inside the Vikings’ receivers room, cosplaying his former career. He crouches. His eyes squint, almost as if he’s transported to a different time.
“If the guy has inside leverage,” McCardell says, “I’ve got to take it away from him. Because that’s where we need to go. And that’s where we’re going to go. Some way, somehow. That’s how we talk in this room. I don’t care who we’re playing. It can be anybody. That’s how it was.”
He returns to his spot sitting atop a desk and eyes the screen once more.
“For Justin, that’s how it is.”
McCardell begins with a 2021 matchup with the Detroit Lions. He wants to start with Jefferson’s route-running creativity.
Because McCardell himself went from being a 12th-round pick to a 16-year NFL veteran — and because his savvy helped him overcome subpar speed — fluidity and suddenness inform his receiver evaluations.
“When I’m watching a guy, it’s always, ‘Is he fluid? Or is he tight?’” McCardell says. “Everything about what Justin does is really super fluid.”
Jefferson flows up the field with a trademark naturalness. McCardell compares Jefferson’s movements to rippling water. At times, McCardell feels it’s his job to give Jefferson guardrails. There is a balance between Jefferson’s playground style and the requirements of a detailed offense built on rhythm and timing.
McCardell pinpoints a crossing route. Here, against the Lions, Jefferson displaces the cornerback off the line of scrimmage. Rather than immediately running toward his destination on the opposite side of the field, Jefferson jabs at the defender to create even more separation.
Is that something he has to do?
McCardell’s mouth peels, a wry smile forming. This is where artistry intersects with convention. Sometimes, allowing someone to bend the rules is necessary to provide them with a platform to showcase their fullest self.
“Like, this is part of who he is,” McCardell says. “A lot of times, on a certain route, I don’t need too much of the sauce. I tell him, ‘Leave the Tabasco where it’s at.”
I’m sure there is a balance with that.
“Oh, yeah,” McCardell says. “A real good balance. I didn’t have his speed, so I was always trying to get to a spot. With him, he has the speed and the sauce. He thinks he needs to nod this guy, which is a little extra, but it also creates more space, so I understand why he did it.”
Justin Jefferson is ELITE.
His route running is a work of art. @JJettas2 | @Vikings pic.twitter.com/2yl8eweRO3
— NFL UK & Ireland (@NFLUKIRE) May 4, 2021
The day after a game, McCardell and Jefferson talk through these intricacies with the rest of the Vikings receivers. In fact, on this specific play, Jefferson notices tight end Tyler Conklin struggling to push vertically, so he adjusts his route to an area that allows for more space.
These explanations, packed with insight, offer an invaluable perspective for young players questioning their own thought processes.
The next clip blips onto the screen, and it’s another Jefferson highlight versus the Lions.
This time, Jefferson leaks past the secondary. Former Vikings quarterback Kirk Cousins hurls a deep ball toward Jefferson in double coverage, and McCardell stops the play. The laser hovers over two Detroit defensive backs in Jefferson’s vicinity.
“Down the field,” McCardell says, “we’re better than these guys at tracking the ball. This is what we do for a living. When we get a ball like this, it should be a catch 80 percent of the time.”
The play continues. Jefferson leaps and snatches the football.
McCardell interjects. Whether he knows the jarring biometrics behind Jefferson’s eye dominance is beside the point.
“His tracking ability is wild.”
… he almost always comes down with these.
“People don’t realize how long he is as a player, either,” McCardell says. “He’s got long arms. He’s taller than you think.”
Minnesota’s offensive staffers use Jefferson to their advantage. For example, most receivers travel 12 to 14 yards on seven-step concepts, but Jefferson’s stride length can take him farther up the field. This adds to his deceptiveness. Cornerbacks often have less time to react than they think they do.
Jefferson’s jump off the line of scrimmage introduces even further panic. Some receivers go through the motions when they’re facing cornerbacks who aren’t pressed up near them at the line of scrimmage. Jefferson sprints after the snap and peels away from defenders with precision.
These are all links in a special chain that get attention only if the receiver makes the catch. And Jefferson usually does, including on this highlight McCardell is now revisiting: the fourth-and-18 snag from 2022 at the Buffalo Bills .
First, McCardell identifies himself on the sideline, jumping when Cousins lobs the ball downfield. Then, he slows the video. Jefferson springs and extends his arm. He palms the ball with one hand, then plucks it away from a defender on the way down.
“When he pulled it down, it was, like, ‘All right, we’re in this thing. He’s on one right now. He’s on a heater,’” McCardell says.
McCardell slaps the wooden desk beside him for effect.
“It doesn’t matter if you’re on the practice squad.” (Bang.)
“It doesn’t matter if you’re the fourth guy on the depth chart.” (Bang.)
“It doesn’t matter if you’re Justin Jefferson.” (Bang. Bang. Bang.)
“This room is open to say poodle to the best player in the room. It’s open to say this to the worst player in the room. It’s always been that way. As a player, if I don’t have respect for the guy playing next to me, knowing he’s going to do his job, then it’s a problem.”
“That’s what we say when you turn down a block,” McCardell says. “Poodle. You’re fluffing up like a poodle. This wouldn’t have been a poodle moment.”
His eyes are on the screen as Jefferson scoots in from his outside receiver position and launches into a block with his shoulder against a Green Bay Packers cornerback. McCardell loves Jefferson’s willingness to stick his face in the fan. He sees it as part of the job description.
You get paid handsomely, McCardell says, for doing things others don’t do. Slithering down the field warrants compensation. Snagging passes over defenders’ helmets does, too. But the top-of-the-market money, in his mind, comes…

full_text:
How quickly will Aaron Judge, who has been out for 100 days, shake off his rust? Ryan Levy / MLB Photos via Getty Images
On paper, the New York Yankees’ struggling lineup received the ultimate boost when the club activated Aaron Judge from the injured list Monday night.
In reality, there are questions Judge and the Yankees will need to answer, starting Tuesday night when he rejoins the team versus the Colorado Rockies at Yankee Stadium.
Here are three things we’re wondering:
The Yankees likely won’t use Judge at full speed right away. It has been 100 days since No. 99 has been in a major-league lineup, as he recovered from fracturing his first right rib while diving to make a catch. He attended the U.S. Open on Monday night, meaning he’s watched more live tennis matches (at least one) than he’s played rehab games (exactly zero). It was Judge’s choice to skip rehab games . On Aug. 27, he told reporters, “Why waste at-bats?”
“Why waste anything down in a minor-league game? I’ve been doing this for a while now, and I’ve got a sense of what I need to do on the field and how to manage it.”
Will Judge spend Tuesday as a designated hitter? Could the Yankees give him essentially a spring training plan on fast-forward, playing him in right field five innings for a couple of games, then seven innings for another few and then progress to full games? Everything seems to be on the table.
Saturday, Yankees manager Aaron Boone told reporters Judge was “in a good spot.”
“He’s physically to the finish line,” the manager said, “where he needs to be. But it’s about just doing it a lot, because that’s ultimately what you’re trying to replicate is being out there for nine innings where you’re playing for three hours and sit down, get up — those kind of things. Just replicating that. So we’re getting to that point with the volume.”
Physically, Judge and the Yankees feel he’s prepared to face big-league pitching and play right field at Yankee Stadium.
But how quickly will Judge shake off his rust?
The 34-year-old has taken steps to get back to game speed, even facing live pitching at Yankee Stadium on Monday afternoon. Judge faced a righty and a lefty, according to video posted by MLB Network. He also stood at the plate with Max Fried on the mound Wednesday at Angel Stadium. Before the Yankees’ recent trip, he hit off the Trajekt high-velocity pitching machine, which uses a video board to simulate deliveries from major-league pitchers .
Aaron Judge taking live BP at Yankee Stadium today.
Via MLB Network pic.twitter.com/Wm3L5CP3rt
— Everything Yankees (@eyyankees) September 7, 2026
Judge also wasn’t able to perform over-the-head movements for a while as his rib recovered, which kept him out of the weight room. It’s unclear whether he’ll return with his usual power and tremendous bat speed.
“Even if it’s a tick off,” Judge said Aug. 27 regarding his bat speed, “I think it’s still better than nothing.”
A point in Judge’s favor? He didn’t play in any rehab games when he missed nearly two months with a toe injury in 2023, and he posted a .965 OPS over his final 57 games.
But at this point in the season, the talk around Judge is usually whether he’ll win another American League MVP, not whether he’ll have enough time to round into playoff shape.
The Yankees have 19 regular-season games remaining. They are four games back of the first-place Tampa Bay Rays and two games ahead of the third-place Boston Red Sox. The Yankees have a nine-game advantage in the wild-card standings, so they are a virtual lock to make the postseason.
Since June 2 — Judge’s first game out of the lineup — the Yankees have combined for a 90 wRC+, the second-worst mark in MLB, behind only the Los Angeles Angels (86). Over that span, they also ranked 26th in runs.
Before that, New York’s 116 wRC+ was second-best in the majors, and it had scored the fourth-most runs.
The Yankees can’t just hope Judge carries them. He’ll likely return to his customary No. 2 slot in the batting order. That could mean sandwiching lefties Ben Rice and Cody Bellinger around him, with Trent Grisham (right hamstring strain) on the injured list.
Rice has been on a tear lately, hitting .358 with a .943 OPS over his last 13 games. Bellinger has hit .293 with a .662 OPS in 14 games since coming off the IL after missing nearly a month with a left hamstring strain. Both should benefit from Judge’s presence.
The Yankees will also need Spencer Jones (.828 OPS over 39 games since being promoted July 26) to continue to hit and play a capable center field in Grisham’s absence .
“To have that right-handed hitter (Judge) on the days we’re facing a righty where we’ve got all our lefties in — to have a right-handed hitter in that two-three hole — I think it goes a long way,” Boone said, “not only having his production back in there, but hopefully putting other guys in a better spot.”

title: Patriots Extend Gonzalez

full_text:
Christian Gonzalez's deal is worth $135 million, making him the highest-paid cornerback in NFL history, and includes $102 million guaranteed. Kenneth Richmond / Getty Images
Christian Gonzalez has agreed to a four-year extension with the New England Patriots, according to league sources who spoke to The Athletic on condition of anonymity early Tuesday because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
The extension is worth $135 million, making Gonzalez, 24, the highest-paid cornerback in NFL history, and includes $102 million guaranteed. It is the largest contract ever given out by the Patriots. Jordan Schultz was first to report the news.
After an incredible season in which he was the backbone of a surging defense that carried the Patriots to a Super Bowl appearance, the contract ensures one of the franchise cornerstones will remain in New England for years to come. It ends a lengthy negotiation between the two sides that lasted several months and left Gonzalez admitting multiple times that he was frustrated .
The two sides had treated Wednesday night’s season-opening game against the Seattle Seahawks as an unofficial deadline for getting an extension done, and now a drawn-out process that lasted the entire summer is finally completed as kickoff looms.
More importantly for the Pats, it locks up arguably their second-most important player as they aim to take advantage of a Super Bowl window pushed open a year ago by Drake Maye and Mike Vrabel.
The Patriots want to build around premium positions, using their last four first-round picks on a pair of offensive tackles, a quarterback and Gonzalez. The cornerback came to the Patriots as the No. 17 pick in 2023 and has been a standout since the start despite playing for three different head coaches in his first three seasons.
Gonzalez had a strong start to his rookie season, but that initial campaign was cut short after four games because of a shoulder injury. He lived up to his billing as a shutdown corner in his second season, earning a second-team All-Pro nod. In 2025, his play improved as the season went along, and Gonzalez played a major role in the team’s magical playoff run. He was one of the few Patriots who played well in the Super Bowl loss to the Seahawks.
Still, it wasn’t easy to get to this point. The negotiations lasted for several months and led to Gonzalez skipping voluntary practices this spring, then not committing in September to whether or not he would play in Week 1 without a new contract. Owner Robert Kraft told the media at the start of training camp that the Patriots had made an offer to make Gonzalez the league’s highest-paid corner , which Gonzalez hadn’t accepted.
Then, after Seattle’s Devon Witherspoon re-set the cornerback market, New England executive VP of player personnel Eliot Wolf reaffirmed that the Patriots had a record-setting offer in front of Gonzalez, who expressed frustration that parts of the negotiation were being made public. After that, Gonzalez’s trainer, Christian White, went on  Boston-based radio station 98.5FM and said some of the language in the Patriots’ contract offer was, “kind of trash.”
Finally, however, the deal is done.
The move also underscores just how poorly the Patriots had selected at the top of the draft before Gonzalez was picked.
Gonzalez is the first Patriots first-round pick to get a second contract with the team since 2012 first-rounder (No. 25 overall) Dont’a Hightower, snapping a run of eight straight top picks not landing a second deal with the team. That’s both a sign of the team’s struggles picking players at the top of the draft in the last decade (a list that includes Malcom Brown, Dominique Easley, N’Keal Harry, and Isaiah Wynn) and a bit of a departure from the way Bill Belichick ran things. Edge rusher Chandler Jones was the last first-round pick who was a no-doubt candidate to be re-signed, but Belichick traded him in an attempt to maximize his value and avoid paying him a lucrative second contract.
It took a lot longer to get to this point than many expected, but it is notable for what it means about how the Patriots are operating. In the 2025 offseason, the Patriots gave Milton Williams a massive contract that made him the highest-paid Patriots player ever. A year later, Gonzalez has that title even if it took months to get there.
And it’ll likely change again soon. Next offseason, Maye is eligible for a contract extension. With another strong season, he won’t be in line just to set a franchise record, but he could become the highest-paid player in NFL history, likely giving the Patriots two of the highest-paid players at their positions (Gonzalez and Maye — plus a potentially redone contract for A.J. Brown). But that’s a topic for another day.
For now, the Pats are pleased to have locked up one of their most talented players, which should help further position them to take advantage of this Super Bowl window.

full_text:
“Can I have a moment alone with Woody?”
The three other men, sitting on couches in Woody Johnson’s office, exchanged looks.
Those close to the Jets’ longtime owner will tell you that he doesn’t like going into a conversation without a sense of what’s to come. In the past, coaches and general managers under his employ tried to avoid that tension. Aaron Glenn walked into it.
Team president Hymie Elhai and the two key consultants of the Jets’ coaching search — Rick Spielman and Mike Tannenbaum — exited. To them, the next few minutes felt like forever.
Then the doors opened. Johnson and Glenn shook hands and it was, for all intents and purposes, done: Glenn would be the next head coach of the New York Jets.
The only two people who know exactly what Johnson and Glenn said that day are the two of them. Whispers posited that Glenn demanded autonomy, that he’d only take the job if Johnson stayed out of his way. That wasn’t quite the truth — the discussion was neither confrontational nor demanding. Glenn was told exactly what he needed to hear.
“When we sat down, he flat-out told me: Listen, I made mistakes,” Glenn tells The Athletic . “I made these mistakes and I’m going to try to make it right. We walked out feeling really good — with a complete understanding.”
And so they forged ahead on a path that Johnson wanted for the organization he purchased for $635 million in 2000. It would be a unified front: A head coach, a GM, a president and an owner, in lockstep. It would require patience — success won’t happen overnight, and it has been many nights since the Jets had any.
Recently, Glenn sat at the end of a long table in a boardroom at the Jets facility and illustrated that point. He positioned his hand at one end of the table.
“You can’t go from here,” he said, then reached his arm all the way out to the opposite end, “to here. You can not skip all these spots (in the middle) to get it going.
“We don’t shake. We don’t rattle to the outside noise because we know exactly what we’re trying to accomplish.”
The wins haven’t shown up yet, but there have been seismic changes in the 19 months since Johnson and Glenn sat in his office. The Athletic spoke with various members of the Jets organization — players, coaches, front office and others (though, through a team spokesperson, Johnson declined an interview request for this story).
Those who work closest with Johnson say he intends to learn from his mistakes and wants to build something sustainable — for his franchise and for his children, who will one day take it over. Many describe a culture that feels like it’s changing for the better. There is a plan. And at its center is a head coach who desperately wants to bring respect back to the organization that drafted him more than three decades ago, and a 79-year-old billionaire who has been roundly blamed for the organization’s failures.
It’s too early to know if the results will change. But those in the building insist that Woody Johnson has.
On a Monday in October 2024, Robert Saleh, still jet-lagged, was in his office watching film and game-planning for the upcoming game against the Buffalo Bills. The Jets had just fallen to 2-3 after a loss to the Minnesota Vikings in London.
On Tuesday morning, Johnson walked into Saleh’s office and fired him . Christopher Johnson, the Jets’ vice chairman and Johnson’s brother, was there too, though he didn’t say anything. Saleh was escorted out of the building; to the coach, to the world, it felt abrupt.
To Woody Johnson, it didn’t. He never clicked with Saleh and made the sole decision to fire him. There were plenty of conspiracy theories swirling about why Johnson fired Saleh when he did, and the way he did, but at the root of the decision was a simple truth: Johnson wasn’t fond of his head coach. The feeling was mutual.
The origin of that antipathy: When Saleh (in January 2021) and GM Joe Douglas (in June 2019) accepted their jobs, it was with the understanding that they would be reporting to Christopher Johnson rather than Woody, who was in London as part of Donald Trump’s first administration, the ambassador to the United Kingdom. Johnson’s return from ambassadorship was jarring for many — even for those who would now consider themselves ardent defenders of Woody Johnson and his leadership style, which can be abrasive and, at times, confrontational compared to his more subdued brother. Woody Johnson wants to understand why things are happening.
Saleh, more conflict-averse by nature, wasn’t a great personality fit for Johnson’s blunt communication style. By the time Saleh was fired, he had long felt kneecapped by an owner who didn’t value his opinion. By then, Douglas was a shell of himself too, often retreating to his office and staying there most of the day. When Douglas joined Saleh in unemployment later during the 2024 season, the two met up one night in New Jersey and celebrated as if they’d just escaped from Shawshank. (Saleh has since been hired by the Tennessee Titans — the Jets’ Week 1 opponent — while Douglas re-joined the Philadelphia Eagles in a player personnel role.)
Johnson had never fired a head coach in-season before, but doing so had its advantages. The Jets brought in Tannenbaum, a former Jets GM himself, and Spielman, a successful GM with the Vikings, to help conduct both the head coach and GM searches in November. Many other teams with vacancies didn’t start that process until January.
“Woody really talked a lot about how he wanted to reset things,” Tannenbaum says. “He wanted to run a very thorough, transparent process and just be open-minded.”
The Jets were thorough. They interviewed 16 head-coaching and 15 general-manager candidates and vetted even more, eliminating many who were deemed to be poor fits in the New York market (including candidates who were hired elsewhere) or for an organization that needed a complete reset. They consulted via Zoom with a handful of former head coaches to pick their brains about what worked, what didn’t and what they’d do differently, a list that included Jay Gruden, Matt Patricia, Jason Garrett, Mike Martz and Chuck Pagano. They consulted with broadcasters who’d spent time in production meetings with all the prospective candidates.
The interview group included Woody Johnson, Christopher Johnson, Elhai, Tannenbaum, Spielman, Woody Johnson’s right-hand man Ira Akselrad and a few other associates from his personal investment company. Tannenbaum and Spielman, at Johnson’s behest, emphasized a uniform interview process for all candidates, eliminating emotional or personal bias, right down to the timing of each interview; every session was an identical length.
“When people make mistakes, it’s because candidate X comes in, and you’re like, ‘Oh my god, what an interview, I’m falling in love with this guy,’” Tannenbaum says. “When you check references or you look at experience or you look at other things you identified as important, and they fall short, you have to adhere to: take emotion out, take recency bias out and let’s keep going.”
Johnson stuck to that. After Glenn won over the room during a rousing virtual interview, a few members of the search committee spent the next few days gushing about how impressive he was. At one point, Johnson told the group to pipe down. “I don’t want to hear about him anymore,” Johnson told them.
In every interview, Johnson addressed the elephant in the room. A few weeks earlier, in December 2024, The Athletic published reporting that depicted him as a meddling owner overseeing a dysfunctional organization. During interviews, he made it clear that whomever the Jets hired would have the autonomy to run the team in their image, that his ultimate goal was to collaborate, not interfere.
Johnson was even open to letting Aaron Rodgers return in 2025 if that’s what his new coach and general manager wanted — even after Rodgers went out of his way to take shots at Johnson and make jokes about his sons on television. While the coach and GM…

title: How Jalen Hurts is preparing for a season that could shape his Eagles future A new offense, a leadership test and an uncertain future: Jalen Hurts enters a pivotal season with the Eagles. Brooks Kubena 4

full_text:
Jalen Hurts’ ability to master a new offense and lead a rebuilt group could help shape his long-term future in Philadelphia. Isaiah Vazquez / Getty Images
The scribble-scratch of a notepad pushed against the silence.
Parks Frazier waited. A quarterbacks coach entering his second year in Philadelphia, Frazier has learned to wait. He knows Jalen Hurts writes everything down. Everything . He has peered at Hurts’ pages and seen “lists on top of lists.” Thoughts in order. Thoughts in rows. Thoughts that form precise questions and more answers on the page.
These notes are part of the process Hurts speaks vaguely about nearly every time he sits behind a microphone.
“Daily deposits,” he calls it. “Daily efforts.” Little by little. List by list. Frazier called Hurts a “relentless note-taker.” This distinct habit — like Hurts’ marathon phone calls with coaches about a week’s given game plan — underlines how the quarterback breaks broad challenges into digestible tasks.
“A challenge is a challenge,” Hurts said on the first day of training camp. “You look at them all the same.”
The 2026 season is a challenge, nonetheless. Compile Hurts’ notes and the lists take form: The greatest schematic challenge of his career. He is not merely playing for his seventh play-caller in seven seasons. The Philadelphia Eagles drastically overhauled their playbook after their offense degenerated in 2025, and the technical and philosophical changes Hurts must master demand a departure from the comfort zones of past systems.
Kevin Patullo’s firing after one year as offensive coordinator headlined the offense’s mismanagement. But a run game that devolved from first-rate to feckless exposed fundamental issues. Coach Nick Sirianni hired another first-time play-caller, Sean Mannion, to build a brand new system with principles championed by Kyle Shanahan and Sean McVay. The Eagles emphasized this reconstruction when they parted ways with longtime offensive line coach and run game coordinator Jeff Stoutland.
Hurts did not emerge unscathed. He regressed in the Patullo-led offense and absorbed multiple reports that his reluctance contributed to the system’s stagnancy. This year’s conditions echo the Eagles’ bounce-back from their 2023 collapse to their Super Bowl LIX championship, when Hurts was named the game’s MVP. If Hurts again rebounds in Mannion’s offense, he will have upheld the confidence Eagles owner Jeffrey Lurie and general manager Howie Roseman have insisted has not wavered. It may even result in a second contract extension, something Lurie and Roseman did not offer Hurts this summer.
And time is a factor not even Hurts can easily ignore. After an Aug. 7 practice, the entire team sang Hurts a happy 28th birthday. He is reaching the age at which NFL teams historically determine whether a quarterback’s peak years are ahead of him — or behind him. Financially speaking, the Eagles can feasibly offload Hurts’ contract after this season. (Or if by trade, during it.)
Hurts avoids addressing such big-picture junctures until they are complete. He politely brushed off a question of such scope in training camp by saying, “Those opportunities that I relish in, they start right now in these moments.” But there was a hint of insight in the way Hurts responded to Lane Johnson’s disclosure that this will be the right tackle’s last season.
“I know it takes great courage to say this is the last dance going into it,” Hurts said.
Hurts does not deny the weight of the past or the future. He simply refuses to let either pull him from the present.
Scrawled within the lines upon lines of Hurts’ notes is an important couplet:
100 percent alignment Zero entitlement
Hurts fit those words into the overall theme of his statements on the first day of training camp. The previous day, Sirianni had opened the Eagles’ team meeting with a message about “being together and being aligned.” Hurts reflected on Sirianni’s message and wrote his couplet on the page.
“I can’t emphasize enough how important it is to carry and protect the intimacy of this team and what we do,” Hurts told reporters. “Because it takes all of us, and we know that there are challenges that come throughout a year.”
It was as close as Hurts came to acknowledging the challenges that sunk them last season — and the locker room frustrations that did little more than trace out a space to brood. The brief life of an inflatable “Positivity Bunny” captured the absurdity of a team that ran out of constructive ways to express their discontent. A.J. Brown was outspoken about his misery, which foreshadowed his trade to the New England Patriots.
The Eagles have moved on. More than a third of their initial 53-man roster is new. DeVonta Smith and Darius Cooper are the only returning members of a revamped wide receiver room. Many of them traveled to Orlando for a workout-and-hang Hurts organized over the summer. Tight end Dallas Goedert, who has been in Philadelphia for Hurts’ entire career, said the trip “was a blast” and that Hurts “took care of us.” For the typically guarded quarterback, organizing it was another outward sign of a more intentional effort to connect with teammates. Goedert said this, grinning through what remained of a mustache that he acknowledged matched Hurts’ new look.
“I think it’ll pay forward,” Hurts said of the trip. “The work will show.”
Josh Grizzard, Philly’s first-year pass game coordinator, has noticed Hurts seeking out teammates in the halls of the team facility or in between plays on the practice field. Grizzard is generally in earshot of the conversations. He has heard Hurts praise targeted receivers when they execute the play correctly. Or explain where they needed to have been. Or describe how the route would need to be adjusted if the defense had played a certain coverage.
“I see him do that every day,” Grizzard said.
During an early August practice, Hurts was unusually expressive after completing a deep pass down the middle to Elijah Moore in tight coverage. Hurts, later explaining his reaction, said that earlier in the practice period, Moore had stopped in the middle of the route, which resulted in an interception.
“That was an example of responding, and that’s what I was so proud of and happy about,” Hurts said. “Not the throw. But that he was able to make the next play, show up in the right window at the right time, and rip it in there for a touchdown in the middle of the field. That’s the M.O. of being a resilient team.”
Hurts’ new relationships build on his oldest: He has known Smith since he was 17; they line danced in Western attire together at Smith’s June wedding. The Eagles believe their established chemistry, which dates back to their college careers at Alabama, will carry and shape the evolution of the passing game.
Hurts, reflecting on their shared history and hunger, said, “He’s saying the same things I’m saying now.”
The Eagles are betting that alignment can help a rebuilt receiving corps backfill Brown’s production. Brown’s $21.8 million dead-cap charge remains the team’s second-largest cap hit in 2026. Roseman balanced the wide receiver budget by spending the No. 20 pick on Makai Lemon and financing veteran depth beyond Smith by taking moderate gambles on Dontayvion Wicks, Hollywood Brown and Moore.
At the center of the new circle is Hurts, whose outreach and availability this summer caught the attention of Moore, A.J. Brown’s teammate at Ole Miss and close friend.
“He’s a person I think that people can learn a lot from,” Moore said of Hurts. “And if you get to know him and get in his circle, I think that he’s someone that you can lean on a lot, if you just open your mouth and ask some questions.”
Mannion often finds himself intrigued when Hurts looks up from his notes to speak.
“He always asks really, really thought-provoking questions,” Mannion said.
The quarterback and play-caller are alike in this way. Ask anyone in the Jefferson Health Complex about Mannion, and the first response will generally be…

full_text:
DK Metcalf says of Antarctica: “I think there is another civilization inside of Earth.” Joe Sargent / Getty Images
Read our exclusive DK Metcalf interview with Jonathan Jones.
DK Metcalf loves conspiracy theories, and he’s not shy about it.
The two-time Pro Bowl wide receiver, who is entering his eighth NFL season and second with the Pittsburgh Steelers, opened up on the topic in a wide-ranging interview with The Athletic’s Jonathan Jones .
“Yeah, I’m a big conspiracy theorist,” Metcalf told Jones. “Shout out to my quarterback.”
One of Metcalf’s most curious theories? He thinks that Antarctica is “another world.”
“I think there is another civilization inside of Earth,” he said.
In his story, Jones did his due diligence by interviewing Brent Christner, a lifelong Steelers fan and an associate professor of microbiology at the University of Florida, who said there is indeed a civilization living inside Antarctica — sort of. Christner said that deep under miles of ice in Antarctica there is water, and living in that water are microbes that have existed for hundreds of thousands of years. These microbes are so infinitesimal that something as small as a crab or slug would be unable to survive off it, however.
“That is one of the problems with being in Antarctica,” Christner says. “Every bit of food, every supply, every needle that you need has got to go south with you.
“The Arctic is a different sort of scenario. There are native peoples that are indigenous to there. And the Arctic is cold, but it isn’t close to being anywhere as cold as Antarctica is.”
It turns out that the Arctic plays into Metcalf’s conspiracy theory as well. Why? It’s a matter of access.
“You can go to Alaska. You could go to the North Pole,” Metcalf said. “But why not Antarctica? Why can’t you just book a trip to Antarctica?”
You can, as Jones points out, book a trip there. Antarctica tourism usually takes place between November and March, and most of it comes via ships leaving from South America and arriving around the Antarctic Peninsula, the northernmost arm of the mainland. There are no commercial airports in Antarctica, however, and the airports that do exist are controlled by governments, which plays right into Metcalf’s theories.
“Why is there a secret meeting — well, it’s not secret,” Metcalf says, “but why is there a meeting between every world leader of every country in Antarctica, specifically?”
There is no verifiable evidence of such meetings taking place. Though, to be fair, off-book meetings of world leaders discussing a secret civilization would have no such records. Besides, a lack of verifiable evidence is what makes conspiracy theories so fun, right?
“There are definitely some distinguished visitors that come down to Antarctica. When they would come down, they would get the royal treatment and get thrown in helicopters and shown all the excellent sites,” Christner says. “But there’s not like a G7 that occurs down there.”
Even Christner says we know more about the surface of Mars than what’s underneath the southernmost point of our planet. Jones, perhaps thankfully, didn’t ask Metcalf about his thoughts on the Red Planet.

full_text:
Brian Fleury replaced Klint Kubiak, who left to be the Raiders' head coach after one season as the Seahawks' offensive coordinator. Steven Bisig / Imagn Images
RENTON, Wash. — As a longtime NFL assistant, Brian Fleury has already lived out a childhood dream.
But when the Seattle Seahawks open the regular season Wednesday night against the New England Patriots, Fleury will achieve a personal milestone: calling plays for the first time as an offensive coordinator. Seattle hired Fleury , previously the San Francisco 49ers’ run game coordinator and tight ends coach, in February to replace Klint Kubiak, who left to become the Las Vegas Raiders’ head coach.
Fleury, who isn’t afraid of a little self-deprecating humor, knew from a young age that his path to the NFL wouldn’t include shoulder pads and a helmet, but a headset and a play sheet instead.
“I wasn’t a very good football player after high school,” Fleury said. “As soon as I realized that (coaching) was going to be the only way I stayed involved, that’s kind of the direction I went.”
Fleury played quarterback at Towson for four seasons but was injured while competing for the starting job with two years of college eligibility remaining. While he was recovering, Fleury got his start in the coaching ranks: He was asked to help prepare the next quarterback in line.
Fleury has since embarked on a coaching journey of more than 20 years, including stops at Sacred Heart as a defensive coordinator and Towson as a special teams coordinator. He called plays in both roles, but he has never done so on offense at any level. Fleury even worked as a football analyst for the Miami Dolphins in 2016, and then as their director of football research from 2017 to 2018, before taking his first full-time job on offense in 2020 as an offensive quality control coach with the 49ers.
“It’s cool to see (Fleury) transition from a tight ends coach who was once (on) defense too,” backup quarterback Drew Lock said. “(To) know the run game, know the blocking, also be able to teach tight ends routes, concepts, why we’re calling these plays — to now be in a position to have his own offense and be able to make his own system, his own image of how he likes to call a game.”
Fleury said at his introductory news conference in February that he’s long been preparing to call offensive plays. The key, he said, is the work done in advance to develop a plan for every situation.
Players often describe Fleury as stoic and dry-humored. Tight end Eric Saubert played for him in San Francisco and adored the coach’s wit back then. To Saubert, though, Fleury stands out much more for his skill than his opportune wisecracks.
“He’s obviously very studied, and you would assume that an offensive coordinator would know everyone’s roles,” Saubert said. “But to be able to articulate it in the moment like he does, I’m telling you: I’ve been on a lot of teams, and not everyone does that, which is pretty cool.”
Fleury noted it’s in his nature to be a bit on the reserved side. He’s authentically himself with his players, often looking ahead and trying to stay ahead rather than getting lost in the moment.
“What’s portrayed on the surface isn’t always what’s going on internally,” he said. “Usually, when something good happens, I’m thinking, ‘On to the next scenario,’ and I’ll celebrate at the end.”
It’s perhaps unsurprising, then, that Fleury hasn’t had much trouble implementing a new offensive system, despite doing so without the luxury of bringing his own assistant coaches to Seattle. Most of the Seahawks’ coaching staff is back in 2025, including three coaches — pass game coordinator Jake Peetz, run game coordinator Justin Outten and tight ends coach Mack Brown — who interviewed for the job that went to Fleury.
“He’s done an unbelievable job,” veteran wide receiver Cooper Kupp said of Fleury. “He didn’t bring anyone with him. He had to install his vision to coaches so they can go out and install it to the players. That’s a tough thing to do, but it’s been cool to have that collaboration.”
Fleury has hardly viewed that task as a chore. As the Seahawks inch closer to their season opener and Fleury’s play-calling debut, he has found Seattle’s most recent practices to be more fun than any from the previous seven years.
Mentors like current NFL head coaches DeMeco Ryans, Robert Saleh and Jeff Hafley all helped Fleury reach this juncture of his career. But he hasn’t heard from many of his advisers of late.
“Unfortunately,” Fleury quipped, “the people I would seek advice from aren’t really interested in seeing us do well.”
The Seahawks, of course, are the reigning Super Bowl champions, and the rest of the league is on high alert for some of Seattle’s most dangerous weapons.
Jaxon Smith-Njigba racked up the eighth-most receiving yards in a single season in NFL history (1,793) last season, winning Offensive Player of the Year. Quarterback Sam Darnold has established himself as a bona fide NFL starter with back-to-back Pro Bowl seasons, growing by leaps and bounds in Fleury’s eyes since he was a backup for the 49ers in 2023.
Fleury, meanwhile, has impressed Darnold with his thorough preparation ahead of Seattle’s Super Bowl 60 rematch.
“Every day we’ve come in so far this week,” Darnold said, “he’s been great in terms of the way he’s presenting, how clear the plan is so far. It’s been great.”
Seattle will naturally adapt its game plan to each opponent, but Fleury’s scheme should be fairly similar to Kubiak’s. The Seahawks are expected to continue using outside-zone principles in the run game and feature plenty of play-action passing from Darnold.
However, defensive lineman Leonard Williams has seen Seattle’s offense lining up much quicker in practice than it did at this time a year ago, and putting tight ends and fullbacks in motion much more frequently.
“It makes it hard on our defense, so there was a lot of good competition throughout camp,” Williams said. “I’m definitely looking forward to seeing how they can continue to grow.”
Running backs could be featured more prominently in the passing game, too, than last season. Kenneth Walker III and Zach Charbonnet combined for 426 receiving yards on 51 catches in 2025.
Reserve running back Emanuel Wilson has run more routes in practice than he usually did across his first three NFL seasons with the Green Bay Packers. Ample opportunities to catch passes out of the backfield could loom for rookie Jadarian Price and third-year pro George Holani.
“It’s wonderful,” Wilson said. “(Fleury is) a great coach, and I love learning from him.”
On Wednesday, Fleury will operate from the sidelines after calling plays on the field for two of Seattle’s three preseason games. He coached from the sidelines the past four seasons in San Francisco as well and enjoys having face-to-face communication with players.
Many of the players Fleury chatted with during preseason games, though, won’t be counted on often during the regular season. He does not expect the lack of game reps to be an issue, nor does tight end AJ Barner, who did not play during the preseason.
When Fleury speaks up, it’s usually for good reason.
“He’s a man of few words,” Barner said. “He’s about ball, about his business.”
It remains to be seen how different Seattle’s offense will be, if at all, considering all the returning players from last year’s Super Bowl-winning squad. Fleury and Kubiak both come from the Kyle Shanahan coaching tree, so the Seahawks’ offense could closely resemble the 2025 version.
That wouldn’t be an unwelcome development. Fleury has arrived in Seattle short on offensive coordinator experience, but with a clear understanding of what the objective is.
“We’re just going to play Seahawk football. That’s what Mike (Macdonald) has always said,” Fleury said. “We’re going to be fast and aggressive — just try to control the game and put pressure on the opponent any way we can.”
Added Lock: “I’m really excited for him. He’s ready for the challenge.”

full_text:
Jaden Dugger (53) showed off his talents with an impressive preseason for the 49ers. Michael Zagaris / San Francisco 49ers / Getty Images
MELBOURNE, Australia — Just five years ago, the roads up the rolling hills and down the steep valleys of Western Pennsylvania would have taken you to Penn Hills High, where, every Friday night, Jaden Dugger would catch touchdown passes — including four in one playoff game — from his younger brother, Julian.
The fans there never would have guessed Jaden would be making his NFL debut at linebacker halfway around the world on Thursday night (Friday morning local time) for the San Francisco 49ers. And while the brothers sensed back then that it was just the beginning, they will never forget those electric evenings.
“Playing with your brother, that’s something a lot of people dream of doing,” Jaden said. “And then to win games, man, it was fun. It’s something I will cherish forever for sure.”
“People in the community always told me there was nothing else like high school football, and I never believed them,” Julian said in a telephone interview. “Until I walked on the field. It was special, plus I had a different connection with my receiver than anybody else.”
Julian, two years younger than 22-year-old Jaden and now a quarterback at Washington State, thought his brother was also a pretty good cornerback and safety. But now the much larger version will be lining up at linebacker against the Los Angeles Rams on national television.
“It’s pretty surreal,” Julian said. “I am very proud of him. I am not going to say I don’t believe it, because I always had the utmost confidence in him. He loved defense, and he ended up putting on a lot of weight in college.”
Many college and NFL scouts didn’t believe, as illustrated by Jaden Dugger’s long journey to Melbourne, where the 49ers are practicing this week ahead of their season-opening game. Now a 6-foot-5, 242-pound linebacker, Dugger began at Georgetown as a no-star recruit playing safety, transferred to Louisiana and transitioned to edge rusher and later inside linebacker, all while putting on 50 pounds.
Dugger was not invited to the 2026 scouting combine, as NFL teams didn’t know where he would fit. That is, until the 49ers reached to draft Dugger — with his 35-inch arms and 84 3/8-inch wingspan — in the fifth round in April.
Part of the reason was that Dugger reminded 49ers linebacker coach and former Seattle Seahawks star K.J. Wright — who measured 6-3 and 246 pounds with 35-inch arms at the 2011 combine — of someone.
“We were in a draft meeting, and K.J. was talking with a lot of conviction on the young man, and I was like, ‘Wait a second …’” general manager John Lynch said after the draft. “‘K.J., you’re trying to draft yourself!’ And we threw up K.J.’s card when he was drafted, and they were very similar.”
Dugger’s versatility and athleticism closed the deal, even if some of the college tape was a little rough at times.
“We believe he can be a really fun player to work with and a really impactful player for our team,” Lynch said.
Defensive coordinator Raheem Morris will use Dugger as a “fever backer,” his term for someone who will cover tight ends, move around and occasionally rush the passer.
Dugger got temperatures rising with a good training camp and a knack for making plays in the preseason, finishing with 10 tackles and two quarterback hits in the finale against the Las Vegas Raiders.
There were also two wince-inducing missed tackles that night, just to underscore that this will be a process. There is no pipeline from the Sun Belt Conference to starting in the NFL.
“I saw a guy out there that looked like he belonged, No. 1, first and foremost,” Morris said. “I saw a guy that showed great length. Saw a guy that showed great range and speed to be able to track and tackle.”
Morris added that Dugger needs to get off blocks faster and to learn when to take a risk, when not to and “when he can absolutely let the trigger go.”
But the rookie is learning every day, with Morris highlighting his communication. And yes, there has been some validation for Dugger the past few months.
“I feel like my whole life, I was underrecruited,” Dugger said. “So, to be picked, kind of like cherished and wanted, it felt good to come in here like that. It was just a different feeling. I loved it, and I am going to do whatever they need me to do.
“Raheem has been challenging me, and I feel I’ve gotten better with my technique and learning the scheme.”
Dugger was recruited by one college (Toledo) as a positionless athlete, but waiting for Penn State or Pittsburgh to make an offer that never came cost him the one he had in hand. He wound up joining Georgetown and started just four games in his first year at a school known for its basketball.
It was there he learned that his 24-year-old brother, Dajuan, died in his sleep on Jan. 23, 2023. Dajuan was the oldest of the five siblings and the reason that Jaden and Julian played football.
“He paved the way for us,” Jaden said. “We followed him every step, and when he got a scholarship (to Lock Haven University), we knew what was possible.”
“He was the biggest inspiration in our family,” added Julian, who started playing football at age 5. “Neither of our parents played sports, nobody in our family really, and he inspired all of us.”
Both brothers said they play the game for Dajuan. Jaden wore No. 3 — his brother’s number — in college and plans to do so with the 49ers once it’s available. (Receiver Christian Kirk is the current occupier; for now, Jaden is wearing No. 53.)
No. 3 suited Jaden well as a safety, but he literally grew out of that position. He still had NFL aspirations when he transferred from Georgetown to Louisiana, even if most around him didn’t see it.
“People were like, ‘C’mon, bro, you’re not going pro,’ and even my junior year wasn’t that great,” he said. “So I knew it was kind of a long shot, but I showed people my senior year that I was serious.”
Dugger had 125 tackles — 13 for a loss — four sacks and an interception for the Ragin’ Cajuns in 2025, earning all-conference honors.
His old high school coach, Jon LeDonne, was not as surprised as you would think to see Dugger become an NFL prospect.
“When I first saw him, I thought we were going to put him at tight end, and he would be Jeremy Shockey,” DeLonne said in a telephone interview. “But he stayed at receiver and defensive back. He had the bigger frame, and you knew he was a great kid and was going to work hard.”
Linebackers Fred Warner and Dre Greenlaw had a similar impression. They took Dugger under their wing this summer, even before training camp started.
“I just learned so much from them, just what they expect out of certain stuff, just certain techniques,” Dugger said.
But that was not the biggest lesson.
“(Their) approach to the game, that’s what’s the most important — being relentless, running to the ball all the time,” Dugger said. “If you watch film, you’re going to see those guys running to the ball all the time. That’s like the 49er way.
“You’re taught that in college, but they don’t harp on it as much. But now … even if you’re 40 yards away, you go chase the ball.”
Now, Dugger appears poised to be the 49ers’ third linebacker, which could mean plenty of work against the Rams and their multi-tight-end packages in the opener. Warner can’t wait to see the rookie in the regular season.
“Dug has a skill set that’s rare,” Warner said. “The fact that he’s a true 6-5, long arms, can run like a deer. He’s not afraid of contact. He can play several different positions. His retention of information, playing with instinct. Those are all things that can get you really excited about a player.”
Kind of like those fans at Penn Hills were five years ago.

title: Tampa Bay Buccaneers watch guide 2026: Schedule, networks for Baker Mayfield's Krewe Here are the dates and channels to know as Tampa tries to reclaim the NFC South title. Jenny Catlin
summary:

The Tampa Bay Buccaneers looked like they could be headed toward another NFC South title when they reached their Week 9 bye at 6-2 in 2025. Now the Bucs try to return to the top of the NFC South.
full_text:
The Bucs have won at least eight games in each season of the 2020s. Mike Ehrmann / Getty Images
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers looked like they could be headed toward another NFC South title when they reached their Week 9 bye at 6-2 in 2025. Instead, they were plagued by injuries, dropped seven of their final nine games and lost the division tiebreaker to the Carolina Panthers. The collapse ended a streak of five consecutive playoff appearances.
Now the Bucs try to return to the top of the NFC South. Todd Bowles is back for his fifth season as head coach, while general manager Jason Licht enters Year 13. The offensive coordinator position, however, is still a revolving door. Zac Robinson replaces Josh Grizzard, giving Tampa Bay its fifth offensive coordinator in five seasons. Robinson has history with quarterback Baker Mayfield from their brief overlap with the Los Angeles Rams in 2022.
For the first time since 2013, the Buccaneers start the season without Mike Evans on the roster. His departure leaves Chris Godwin, Jalen McMillan and Emeka Egbuka atop the receiving corps. Egbuka led Tampa Bay in receiving as a rookie. Bucky Irving is also healthy again, though the team added Kenneth Gainwell to fortify the backfield.
Tampa Bay’s defense won’t look the same, either. Bowles continues to run the defense himself, but the personnel around him changed considerably after a difficult 2025 season in which the red-zone defense ranked last in the NFL. Lavonte David retired after 14 seasons, leaving another major piece to replace. The Buccaneers signed linebacker Alex Anzalone, defensive lineman A’Shawn Robinson and edge rusher Al-Quadin Muhammad. They also used the No. 15 overall pick on Miami edge rusher Rueben Bain Jr. and a second-round pick on linebacker Josiah Trotter.
Tampa Bay is currently scheduled to have three primetime games. The final three weeks are all TBD, though, including two NFC South showdowns. If the division comes down to the last week again, it’s possible the Bucs will have another national spotlight.
Check out the full TV guide below and be sure to follow the Buccaneers on The Athletic , along with NFL coverage from “ The Athletic Football Show ” and Scoop City , throughout the season.
All times listed below are ET.
The most expansive option for live game coverage is a multichannel plan. That includes streamers like Fubo, Sling TV and YouTube TV, or more traditional providers like DirecTV, Dish and Xfinity. We lay out cord-cutting alternatives for each NFL media partner down below, but there’s a certain peace of mind to the consolidation of pay television.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, AFC Championship Game
Each week, CBS carries games across two Sunday kickoff slots: one at 1 p.m., and another at 4:05 p.m. or the national window at 4:25 p.m. There will be 10 nationwide Sunday doubleheaders this year on CBS. Broadcasts are set by region when there are multiple offerings in a spot.
It’s not a clean split, but CBS is known as the primary home of the AFC. The network’s theme music is a certified slapper.
Its main pregame show, “The NFL Today,” adds recent retirees Russell Wilson and Kyle Long to its studio crew. CBS announcers include Jim Nantz and Ian Eagle, while the color commentary rotation stars JJ Watt.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an indoor TV antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local CBS games also stream on Paramount+.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, NFC Championship Game
Like CBS, Fox splits Sunday afternoons between early 1 p.m. action and later 4:05/4:25 p.m. matchups. Its centerpiece is branded as “America’s Game of the Week.” Unlike CBS, Fox has a dancing robot named Cleatus . It’s the nominal network for the NFC as well.
Kevin Burkhardt, Joe Davis and Adam Amin are the lead play-by-play voices. Burkhardt pairs with Bucs franchise savior Tom Brady , while Davis calls games alongside Greg Olsen. Amin is partnered with newcomer Drew Brees, who is fresh off his Pro Football Hall of Fame induction. Some Spanish-language broadcasts are available on Fox Deportes.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local Fox games also stream on Fox One.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (out-of-market fans)
These two are the access points for all non-national matchups that aren’t on regional CBS or Fox.
NFL Sunday Ticket has full games. It’s exclusive to YouTube and YouTube TV. Those without a YouTube TV plan can still get NFL Sunday Ticket as a primetime channel through the standard YouTube app.
RedZone is the whip-around program that jumps around the slate to cover scoring drives. This is the place for Scott Hanson , “the witching hour” and chaotic octobox split screens. It can be added to NFL Sunday Ticket, and it’s included on some high-end pay TV sports plans.
RedZone also lives on NFL+ Premium, which can be bundled with the ESPN Unlimited plan.
What you’ll need to watch: An NFL Sunday Ticket subscription through YouTube TV or the YouTube app; NFL RedZone access through select pay TV packages, ESPN Unlimited or NFL+ Premium.
Playoffs: 2 wild-card games, 1 divisional game
This is the faithful home of “Sunday Night Football” each weekend. And because everything has to be confusing, the NBC lineup opens with a Wednesday night season premiere. At least SNF has a consistent 8:20 p.m. start time.
Mike Tirico and Cris Collinsworth are in the booth, with Melissa Stark reporting from the sidelines. Carrie Underwood sings about waiting all day for Sunday night . NBC’s “Football Night in America” pregame show brings on longtime head coach Mike Tomlin. Telemundo has the telecasts in Spanish.
The network has two extra Saturday offerings for Week 17. One is exclusive to Peacock, and both matchups will be announced later in the season. The same goes for NBC’s Week 18 regular-season finale.
“Sunday Night Football” is subject to flex scheduling — games can be swapped in and out of the window twice between Weeks 5-10 and any time from Weeks 11-17. This allows executives to pick games with greater playoff implications, though it leaves the actual ticket holders in a bind.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing, or a Peacock account with the live sports plan.
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, Super Bowl LXI
The Disney networks combine to cover 17 “Monday Night Football” games. Ten of those are on both ABC and ESPN, with another seven exclusive to the latter. The Buccaneers play in the final Monday night game of November when they host the Panthers in Week 12; it airs on ESPN only. The oft-maligned “Monday Night Football” doubleheader is now a thing of the past, at least.
MNF kickoffs have 8:15 p.m. starts, and their schedule flexes can happen any time in Weeks 12-17. The two Saturday ABC/ESPN matchups in Week 18 will be set as the postseason picture sharpens.
ESPN is preparing for its first Super Bowl broadcast ever on Feb. 14, 2027. It will be simulcast on ABC.
Joe Buck handles play-by-play for MNF. He’s joined by analyst Troy Aikman, plus the sideline duo of Lisa Salters and Laura Rutledge. Spanish-language airings can be found on ESPN Deportes. For 12 regular-season games and the Super Bowl, ESPN2 offers an alternate “ManningCast,” in which Eli and Peyton Manning watch the games with famous fans. Guests have ranged from Bill Belichick to Lil Wayne .
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for ABC, or an ESPN Unlimited account.
Main window: Thursday night
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game
Most weeks begin with “Thursday Night Football,” which kicks off at 8:15 p.m. Those games are behind the Prime paywall, but they’re free over the air in the participants’ home markets. Flex rules around TNF are a bit less hectic, with two allotments between Weeks 13-17.
The Bucs are set to appear on TNF once…
